Title: b'fingoldo'
Body:
b'Could we change SQL tables layout to support more than one embedding, potentially from more than one provider? As I see it, problem is that the documents table has only one unique vector_id field, and different retrievers can create arbitrarily vector IDs. But we could use as many vector_ids fields as we need, in theory.

I actually don't know the reason of limiting all work to only one "text" field. Let's say I am working with scientific papers. I can have many text fields: title, abstract, full_text, reviews. And I can already load all of them into Haystack. But why am I limited to working (creating embeddings, querying) with only one of those fields, which I should decide upfront and can not change without re-importing WHOLE collection each time?

It would be so logical from the end user's point of view, at the update_embeddings() step, to pass a **field_name** parameter (to specify the exact field they want to create embeddings for) and **embedding_name** parameter to be able to use more than one model or even vector storage engine for that field, and find the right tradeoff between accuracy vs storage/compute requirements, all that without reimporting possible millions or billions of documents for no reason.

embedding_name by default could serve as a convenient label, I would suggest bookkeeping of the retriever model metadata (model, vector_dim, vector store) in a separate table. When no embedding_name is provided by the user, the retriever can still be matched by that metadata and results would go to the correct DB field without wasting disk space.

We actually could lower requirements a lot by allowing Haystack users to connect to any pre-loaded and existing DB table by specifying its name in the doc store init() method, no?

We would only need to maintain a table of **_embeddings_** _(id primary key serial, table_name, field_name, model_metadata,vectors_created_at,vectors_updated_at,vectors_queried_at,user_metadata) unique (table_name, field_name, model_metadata)_
and a table of **_vector_ids_** _(embedding_id references embeddings(id),document_id,vector_id) unique(embedding_id,document_id)_.

PROS:
ability to work with existing tables
ability to work with multiple text fields as first-class citizens
ability to quickly switch between different embedding generation models
ability to track stats (how many time embeddings creation took, hardware used, what was the accuracy for each model/method, etc)

CONS:
a few extra parameters
additional method to delete vector ids not unused for a long time

What am I missing? )'

Title: b'tholor'
Body: b'Agree. Creating embeddings for multiple text fields could be helpful. Not sure yet how to handle this in the best way in the retrieval stage, but I think we can figure something out (either aggregating sim. scores from multiple retrievals or the user can simply change the targeted field). Added a new issue for this #1548. '

Title: b'Prepare non-English SQuAD '
Body:
b"I saw that you released GermanQuAD. (https://huggingface.co/datasets/deepset/germanquad)
Could you share some details on how you prepared the dataset?
I want to train a monolingual Dutch QA model. I plan to use an existing pre-trained Dutch BERT base model, and prepare some Dutch SQuAD samples myself. I have following ideas,
1) machine translation of English SQuAD.
2) human annotation of 500 Dutch question-passage-answer (Q-P-A) triplets in my domain.

If I skip 2), would 1) already be enough?
If I add 2), would 500 Q-P-A samples be enough?
By enough I mean at least better than a multilingual model.

I've tried the multilingual model `deepset/xlm-roberta-large-squad2` on my Dutch samples. It works a bit however the performance is not satisfactory, which is expected. I feel that training a monolingual Dutch QA model will be much better. Your advice and tips are much appreciated!"

Title: b'bogdankostic'
Body:
b'Hi @yingzwang! We released a [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.12741) where we summarize our learnings from creating the GermanQuAD dataset. We saw that using human annotations instead of machine-translated labels results in a better performance and also did some experiments on how the number of training samples affects the performance (see Figure 3).
Also, we released a [blogpost](https://medium.com/deepset-ai/going-beyond-squad-part-1-question-answering-in-different-languages-8eac6cf56f21) about QA on different languages than English.

Let me know if you have further questions :)'

Title: b'yingzwang'
Body:
b"Thanks for sharing the paper @bogdankostic ! At a quick glance I see a lot of useful stuff that's exactly what I'm looking for.
The result of Table 4 is a bit surprising to me. The monolingual model trained on translated SQuAD is even worse than the XLM model trained on English SQuAD! Is the machine translated SQuAD that bad? I manually checked a few machine translated (English-to-Dutch) SQuAD samples, and they look pretty OK, i.e., the translated text is quite accurate and natural. What could seriously go wrong with the machine translated SQuAD, so that the monolingual model cannot learn well? 

The performance boost by human annotated GermanQuAD is significant. I'm encouraged to invest more effort preparing more human annotated DutchQuAD :) Also need to explore a bit your annotation tool.

"

Title: b'yingzwang'
Body: b'Also in the paper you mentioned about "detailed labeling instructions". Could you share your complete labeling instructions? Or is it already everything in Appendix A?'

Title: b'julian-risch'
Body:
b"Hi @yingzwang Appendix A contains all labeling instructions, yes. As we had a team of annotators, we did regular meetings during the annotation process where we discussed newly annotated samples. For example, we discussed the phrasing of the question and whether we can rephrase the question so that there is less lexical overlap with the answer string. Another example is that we discussed whether the question is self-sufficient or whether there should be some additional information in the question for open-domain question answering.

English-to-Dutch machine translation of SQuAD should already give you quite good results. At first glance, the translations look very good, I agree. However, sometimes there are small mistakes or the words used in the translation do not really fit the context. Sometimes machine-translation could increase the lexical overlap of the question and the answer and thus simplify the task for the model. That might be one reason why training on machine-translated data is not as good as training on carefully hand-annotated data. 

I think 500 hand-annotated samples could already be enough to see an improvement, yes. I would recommend that you try to make these 500 samples not too simple for the model.

Please keep us updated about the progress of your project and don't hesitate to contact us again if there are any questions coming up. Feel free to close the issue for now if there are no further questions at the moment and re-open it later. Good luck with training a monolingual Dutch QA model!  "

Title: b'yingzwang'
Body:
b'Thanks for the elaborated answer @julian-risch ! You have really adopted a robust quality control workflow. How large is your annotation team? Not sure if I can afford a similar setup but I'll try.

I found the manual of your annotation tool [here](https://haystack.deepset.ai/guides/annotation). There's one rule saying "Dont create question that elaborate on context", in page 13. Why is that? A user is very likely to ask a question in that way, especially in a conversation. Why should we avoid it in training data?

Your labeling instructions are insightful. From ~50 annotated samples I've collected so far, some already violated the "no lexical overlap rule" and "prefer short answer over long answer rule". I read your paper just in time :)'

Title: b'julian-risch'
Body: b"Great to hear that you find our documentation helpful! @yingzwang \r\nQuestions shouldn't have too many words in common with the context around the answer because that simplifies the question answering task and simple questions are not very helpful for the training. You are right, that users might ask such questions in an application. That's no problem for the model as it is a simple task to then find the corresponding document and answer. There is no need for training data that represents this relatively simple task.\r\nWe had a team of five annotators when we created the GermanQuAD dataset. Having a team of annotators does not only speed up the annotation process. It also helps at formulating more diverse questions and answers. For that reason I would recommend to have at least two annotators."

Title: b"Unintuitive behavior of reader's top_k"
Body:
b'**Describe the bug**
We have various params to control the number of answers returned from the reader: 
- `top_k_per_sample` => max answers coming from one sample (i.e. lowest level; one snipped of max_seq_len)
- `top_k_per_candidate` => max answers from one doc
- `top_k` => total max answers (highest level; results returned to the user)

Problem 1: 
If you have short indexed documents (e.g. when using DPR), you get in many cases less than the expected `top_k` answers as `top_k_per_sample=1` per default. We should rethink the default or make this somehow clearer in the docs.
  
Problem 2: 
In the demo UI, I tested two cases: 
a)  `top_k_reader = 5` and `top_k_retriever=3`
b)  `top_k_reader = 4` and `top_k_retriever=3`

I would expect that the answers 1-4 are identical in both cases and only the last one from a) gets removed in b). 
However, some other results also seem to change: 

a)
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1563902/107938033-0af39080-6f85-11eb-90c2-2062ec9cd5a7.png)

b)  
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1563902/107938080-1e9ef700-6f85-11eb-9d4d-0aae5711ef49.png)

**To Reproduce**
`docker-compose up` on latest master

**System:**
 - OS: Ubuntu 18-04
 - GPU/CPU: CPU
 - Haystack version (commit or version number):  latest master
'

Title: b'Timoeller'
Body:
b'Agreed, this behavior is quite confusing : ) What is uncommon is to have more reader answers than retrieved candidate passages.

So I quickly ran tests with:
```
pipe.run(query="Who is the father of Arya Stark?", top_k_retriever=10, top_k_reader=4)
[   {'answer': 'Eddard'},
    {'answer': 'Lord Eddard Stark'},
    {'answer': 'Ned'},
    {'answer': 'Joffrey'}]


pipe.run(query="Who is the father of Arya Stark?", top_k_retriever=10, top_k_reader=5)
[   {'answer': 'Eddard'},
    {'answer': 'Lord Eddard Stark'},
    {'answer': 'Ned'},
    {'answer': 'Joffrey'},
    {'answer': 'Robb'}]
```
which makes sense again.

I see two points for improvement:
- [quick fix] give a warning if top_k_retriever < top_k_reader
- use the new FARM QAPredictionHead parameter `duplicate_filtering` to filter out similar answers and increase values for top_k_per_sample and top_k_per_candidate


Should I implement both methods? Do you see other ways for improvement? 
I would prefer to not change the underlying FARM QA parameters based on topk haystack values, this might lead to really strange behavior.


---------------
Additional info from the FAMR docs for the passage filtering parameter:
Answers are filtered based on their position. Both start and end position of the answers are considered. The higher the value, answers that are more apart are filtered out. 0 corresponds to exact duplicates. -1 turns off duplicate removal.'

Title: b'Krak91'
Body:
b"Hi. I'm trying to wrap my head around this and figure out what the best configuration is for my use case.
From what I understand, it goes as follows:

1. Retriever gets x amount of documents (candidates) from document store
2. Each document is split to smaller samples (IF its length is more than **max_seq_length**)
3. For each sample reader gets the **top_k_per_sample** top predictions
4. Predictions are grouped by Document (candidate), and for each Document get the **top_k_per_candidate** top predictions
5. Aggregate all predictions
6. Get the **top_k** top predictions from step 5.
And the predictions are picked based on their probability/score..

The issue described above is interesting and I'd like to understand how/why it came up with different answers, or more answers than the number of candidates. 

Let's consider my case where I split and index the files to passages with length <= **max_seq_len**. A few questions:
1. If a candidate fits in the model, is it then considered a sample? Which will apply to the predictions? **top_k_per_sample**, or **top_k_per_candidate**? 
2. If a candidate fits in the model and the **top_k_per_sample** is set to the default 1, will the value of **top_k_per_candidate** still have some kind of effect?
3. Given that all my candidates are small and the model can process each one as a whole, and if they indeed are limited by **top_k_per_sample**, is it better to set it to 2, or 3? The thinking behind it is that a good answer might be skipped from one candidate/sample that would have higher probability than answers from other candidates/samples.
4. In my case, I aim to get the top 3 answers from a set of documents where each document is less than **max_seq_len**. What would you suggest to be the best values for these parameters?"

Title: b'bogdankostic'
Body:
b'Hey @Krak91! Let me try to answer your questions:

> 1. If a candidate fits in the model, is it then considered a sample? Which will apply to the predictions? top_k_per_sample, or top_k_per_candidate?

Yes, if a candidate contains less tokens than max_seq_len, it is not further split into samples, but is one sample. Usually, we would recommend to set top_k_per_candidate a bit higher than top_k_per_sample, but in this case it would make sense to set them to the same value.

> 2. If a candidate fits in the model and the top_k_per_sample is set to the default 1, will the value of top_k_per_candidate still have some kind of effect?

In this case, top_k_per_candidate would not have an effect, as the model would return only 1 answer per sample and therefore also only 1 answer per candidate is available.

> 3. Given that all my candidates are small and the model can process each one as a whole, and if they indeed are limited by top_k_per_sample, is it better to set it to 2, or 3? The thinking behind it is that a good answer might be skipped from one candidate/sample that would have higher probability than answers from other candidates/samples.

This might be something that is worth trying out and see whether this will improve the answers on your specific documents. However, the predictions on sample level are usually very similar. 

> 4. In my case, I aim to get the top 3 answers from a set of documents where each document is less than max_seq_len. What would you suggest to be the best values for these parameters?

In this case, you should set `top_k` to 3 and `top_k_per_sample` and `top_k_per_candidate` to the same value.'

Title: b'bogdankostic'
Body:
b'Hi @anurag89sharma, thanks for sharing the notebook! In haystack, questions are normalized, this means that if the questions end with a question mark, the question mark is removed.

This results in different inputs, for example, using the transformers library, the model will get as input `"hello , is my dog cute ?"` while with haystack, the model will get as input `"hello , is my dog cute "`. If you remove the question marks from your queries, you should get the same embeddings using the transformers library and haystack.

Does this  explanation answer your question? :)'

Body:

I have updated the [notebook](https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1As8HKgsS7bG3bjLb95riwzgBE1r_DN9q) if you want to look at it again. The difference is small but its still there. Title: b'bogdankostic'
Body:
b"I would say that the difference is so small that I would consider the embeddings still as same. In fact, the embeddings haystack produces are equal to the ones produced in transformers until [this line of code](https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/d3fd888a766f4b197a4c26c9346f290cbc71048a/haystack/retriever/dense.py#L258), where we transform the PyTorch tensors to Numpy arrays. 

With regard to the normalizing of questions: Haystack is doing this automatically, so you don't need to worry about this. We decided to do this because the questions in the DPR dataset don't contain a question mark either.

We recommend using `dot_product` as a similarity metric for DPR (see [here](https://haystack.deepset.ai/components/retriever#dense-passage-retrieval-recommended)). In case you want to use `cosine` similarity metric, you can use `FAISSDocumentStore` where the vectors are normalized for you."

Title: b'Timoeller'
Body:
b'Hey sorry for the late reply, I actually had to dig into the code a bit.
So there are two ways to load models.

## Loading model with internet access
The easiest is just to load a QAInferencer with your model name supplied. Then it downloads and converts everything you need. You can do that with:
`infer = QAInferencer.load(model_name_or_path="wptoux/albert-chinese-large-qa", task_type="question_answering", gpu=True)`

Then you can save and load that Inferencer with .save(foo/bar) and .load(foo/bar)

## Loading transformers model saved locally
If your transformers model happens to be saved locally (e.g. with git lfs cloning) and you do not have internet access at that machine you have to construct the FARM Reader model a bit. Here is the code for it:
```
from farm.modeling.adaptive_model import AdaptiveModel
from farm.utils import initialize_device_settings
from farm.infer import Inferencer, QAInferencer
from farm.data_handler.processor import SquadProcessor
from farm.modeling.tokenization import Tokenizer
from pathlib import Path
device, n_gpu = initialize_device_settings(use_cuda=True)

model_name = "local_models/xlm-roberta-base-squad2"

# Load a Tokenizer
tokenizer = Tokenizer.load(
    pretrained_model_name_or_path=model_name
)
# stick it into a Processor
label_list = ["start_token", "end_token"]
processor = SquadProcessor(
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
    max_seq_len=256,
    label_list=label_list,
    data_dir=Path("../data/squad20"),
)

# Convert the local transformers model to FARM style
model = AdaptiveModel.convert_from_transformers(model_name,device=device,task_type="question_answering")

# Put everything into a Inferencer - at this point you have a ReaderModel
infer = Inferencer(model=model,processor=processor,task_type="question_answering")


# Testing the Reader Model
QA_input = [
    {
        "questions": ["Who counted the game among the best ever made?"],
        "text": "Twilight Princess was released to universal critical acclaim and commercial success. It received perfect scores from major publications such as 1UP.com, Computer and Video Games, Electronic Gaming Monthly, Game Informer, GamesRadar, and GameSpy. On the review aggregators GameRankings and Metacritic, Twilight Princess has average scores of 95% and 95 for the Wii version and scores of 95% and 96 for the GameCube version. GameTrailers in their review called it one of the greatest games ever created."
    }]
print(infer.inference_from_dicts(dicts=QA_input)[0])
```


Btw what are you using this model for? Are you using it in haystack? '

Title: b'QA model confidence'
Body:
b'The QA answer score that is currently implemented can be misleading if not downright wrong. Lets create a "score" or confidence that is more informative.

The detailed plan how to approach QA model confidence follows soon.

Related issue on haystack side: https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/issues/739'

Title: b'julian-risch'
Body:
b'**First Plan**
We would like a QA model to state something like with confidence of 75% the predicted answer is correct.
Here comes a first simple plan based on a technique called temperature scaling. Further improvements could follow later on. The approach works not only for extractive QA but also for classification tasks. An adaptation of the approach might also work for Open Domain QA and RAG.

Current scores given for each generated answer combine the logits of the start and end index into one full answer score but do not really correspond to the models confidence. I suggest to scale (calibrate) these logits so that the scaled score corresponds to the accuracy (or other metrics) with which start and end indices are predicted correctly on a validation dataset. Thus, the model learns to output confidence scores that are calibrated on the observed confidence on a validation dataset.

The classification tasks (not QA), the idea is also described here: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.04599.pdf 
There is an implementation available here: https://github.com/gpleiss/temperature_scaling 

It comes down do adjusting the scores based on the following formula:
`softmax = e^(z/T) / sum_i e^(z_i/T)`
`T` is the temperature for scaling, learned based on the validation dataset
`z` is the logit for start index (or end index) as predicted by the model

For extractive QA, we would end up with two confidence scores, one for the start index and one for the end index. We need to try out different ways of combining them in one single score. 

@lalitpagaria  What do you think about the idea? Would you be interested in collaborating with us on this issue? We could schedule a call to discuss model confidence and the suggested plan. Integration with RAG seems to be more complex. Maybe right after the beam search step, when probabilities for each hypothesis are calculated, is a good point to use temperature scaling and output confidence scores.'

Title: b'Similarity based Evaluation of QA Answer'
Body: b'Research options to evaluate answers based on semantic similarity.'

Title: b'Timoeller'
Body:
b"We made some experiments with pretty promising results:

# Model
There is already a pretrained `SentenceTransformer('T-Systems-onsite/cross-en-de-roberta-sentence-transformer')`
I suspect training a joint model with our TextPairClassification can give only minor improvements. If this turns out to be used a lot, we could still train one, since in this scenario we do not gain much from the indexing capabilities.

## Eval on German
GermanQuAD test set annotations, only took answers coming from completely different text positions.
Computed embeddings with the sentencetransformers + cosine sim.
Checked all 40 answer pairs with cosine sim > 40, all texts seemed to semantically match:
- 'Sechste Generation', '6. Generation'
- 'Der Berstwiderstand gibt den bentigten Druck an, um ein Papier zum Bersten zu bringen.', 'Druck, der zum Durchstoen des Papiers erforderlich ist'
- 'Wichtig ist, dass jeder gegnerische, passempfangsberechtigte Spieler gedeckt ist', 'beinhaltet alle Spieler, die die gegnerischen Spieler decken, die einen Pass fangen drfen'

## Eval on English
Same model applied to SQuAD dev set. Checked 180 answer pairs above cosine sim 0.7. All texts seemed to match:
- 'Parliament of the United Kingdom', 'The British Parliament'
- 'the convecting mantle', 'convection of the mantle'
- 'prime ideals', 'prime elements' (slightly unsure without context)
- 'nineteenth-century cartographic techniques', 'nineteenth-century maps'

## Modelling errors
The model seems to be a bit sloppy when it comes to numbers and dates.
- 'oxygen-18', 'oxygen-16'
- '1562', '1564'
- 'January 2010', 'February 2011'
But this could be handled with postprocessing or a couple of training examples, which are easy to generate.

## Detecting labelling errors
When looking at the other spectrum of dissimilar answers we might have a tool here for improving annotations much more easily.
Examples of sims below 0.2 are:
- 'Schrdinger', 'Newtonian equations'
- 'conservation of mechanical energy', 'the tension force on a load can be multiplied'
- 'global', 'in space'
- 'poor harvest', 'allegedly corrupt machinations of Franois Bigot'

# Implementation
Looking at the code I believe a registered metric might be the best case, since we want to parameterize the evaluation with models and a threshold for deciding if a prediction is close to the given gold labels."

Title: b'Implement Similarity based Answer evaluation'
Body:
b'Following up on research done in deepset-ai/FARM#757 

### Target Approach
Implementing a new registered metric using the sentencetransformers model.
Also implement a default metric for FARM with default model. Look for ways to pass comparison model to FARM.

### Implementation details
Input to our metric functions, preds and labels, are in number format.
Preds are of type QACandidate, but missing text answer information.
Labels are tuples of start and end indices.

Our evaluator.eval pipeline is not meant for dealing with plaintext predictions or labels because we dismiss our "baskets" with all text information. Also using the tokenizer to detokenize input_ids (token ids) will not work since we do not collect input_ids in the evaluator. Therefore we should start an initial implementation based on Inferencer output and not create a default FARM metric.'

Title: b"Migrate from apex to Pytorch's native AMP"
Body:
b"**Is your feature request related to a problem or particular use case?**
We initially implemented AMP via Nvidia's apex. Since a while PyTorch supports it natively (see [here](https://pytorch.org/blog/accelerating-training-on-nvidia-gpus-with-pytorch-automatic-mixed-precision/)). Let's migrate as apex was always a painful dependency to install/maintain.

All written documents should have unique vector_ids

```

All system

Title: b'Inconsistency among restart policies in `docker-compose.yml`'
Body:
b"**Describe the bug**
In `docker-compose.yml`, only the `haystack-api` container has a restart policy of `always`, while all other containers don't. This leads to the strange situation where, if the containers are not turned off manually, at every reboot this single container will spawn up on its own.

**Expected behavior**
Either all containers come up (so that the resulting system is usable) or none of them. I personally lean for the second option: this `docker-compose.yml` is for a quickstart example, not a production system.

**To Reproduce**
`docker-compose up` in the root folder, then reboot your machine. At boot, running `docker ps` will show you that `haystack-api` is up."

Title: b'Add cosine similarity as similarity metric for FAISS document store'
Body:
b"**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
FAISS is a really nice and fast indexing solution for dense vectors. Using it for semantic similarity search works very well. However, currently only dot product and L2 are supported when it comes to distance metrics for FAISS. In https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/7569ab97dde4e116ba9e24fcffcf6276c0dbd370/haystack/document_store/faiss.py#L98 you raise an error whenever any other distance metric should be used for FAISS indices. When looking at sentence embedding models which are currently available, only some of them are optimized for dot product similarity (mostly for asymmetric search) while most work well with cosine similarity (mostly for symmetric search) (see https://www.sbert.net/docs/pretrained_models.html#sentence-embedding-models ). It would be really nice if the FAISS document store could also support cosine similarity as a distance metric.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
As stated in the FAISS documentation (https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/MetricType-and-distances#how-can-i-index-vectors-for-cosine-similarity) dot product is equivalent to cosine similarity when the indexed vectors and the query vector are normalized. This feature could be implemented by normalizing all documents which are written by a FAISS document store which was initialized with a cosine similarity metric. The same would have to be done for the retriever.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
-
**Additional context**
I could try and make a PR for this, if such a feature is desired. I'd also be glad if you had any hints on your preferred way of implementation.
"

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b"Hey @mathislucka , 
This would be a very helpful addition - we'd be happy to see a PR here :) 

We'd probably need to add the normalization to `write_documents` (if docs already contain embeddings), `update_embeddings` and `query_by_embedding` when the doc store was initialized with cosine similarity. I currently don't see the need to touch the retriever, but maybe I am missing something."

Title: b'lalitpagaria'
Body:
b'@tholor we reverted this in https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/pull/467. Refer https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/pull/422  for more discussion. Referring comment -

> After some further investigation, I think we can actually get rid of the phi normalization trick.
> The HMSW Index in FAISS now also supports the inner product metric directly. While I had problems with initializing the index via the factory the direct init seems to work well (facebookresearch/faiss#1434).
> When comparing both approaches, it seemed that L2+ Phi normalization is a bit faster (0.009 vs. 0.006 sec/query), but accuracy was actually a bit worse on some random dummy vectors (~ 0.85 vs 0.54) .
> 
> 

'

Title: b'tholor'
Body: b'This was a different type of normalization. If I recall correctly we used L2+Phi normalization back then to enable inner product in HNSW. This was then later on natively supported by FAISS and the trick was not required anymore. This issue here however is about supporting cosine similarity (just requiring L2 normalization). '

Title: b'mathislucka'
Body: b"You are right @tholor there will probably only be changes in the document store and not in the retriever. I didn't look at it properly before. I'll make sure to read through the referenced issues when implementing the feature.\r\n\r\nWhat do you think about the case when someone loads an existing faiss index from a file. As far as I can see, no initialization parameters are saved alongside the file so someone might initialize an index that was originally generated with cosine similarity with another distance metric. This would produce incompatible vectors. Currently, I am not sure if there is a solution to this. On the other hand, you already put responsibility to check if saved and loaded indices are compatible in the hands of the end user (e.g. here: https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/07bd3c50ead83ec934fcc9eaf425b7dca44add79/haystack/document_store/faiss.py#L454). So maybe it would be Ok to place the burden on the user here."

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b"> What do you think about the case when someone loads an existing faiss index from a file.

Good point. It might make sense to add the `similarity` arg to the `load` method. Then it's still the users responsibility to check that the right one is set, but at least it's possible to set it. 
Optionally, we could also do a check after the index is loaded and similarity = cosine - We could verify that a sample of vectors has length = 1 and was therefore normalized. "

Title: b'mathislucka'
Body:
b"I didn't get to writing any code but I manage to think a bit more about the issue of embedding mismatch when loading a faiss document store by calling its `load` method:

As far as I can see, the `load` method does not take the same arguments as the `__init__` method. Isn't this problematic because the document store will always be initialized with the default values when using the `load` method? I mean, it's not just the `similarity` arg that would be missing, it's also all the other arguments.

I came to the conclusion that the `load` method should take the same args as the `__init__` and pass them during initialization. I think this should be a separate PR though.

From an end user perspective, I do not like that I have to remember these arguments or store them somewhere else. Couldn't the `save` method also save the current configuration of the document store alongside the actual faiss index file? We could just store it in a json or something. Maybe make this optional and the `load` method will either look for such a file when loading the faiss index or it will use the default args. This would also be non-breaking as indices which were saved without configuration would still load in the same way as before. This would also be a separate PR I think.

What do you think about this @tholor ?"

Title: b"faiss document store should save it's configuration alongside the index"
Body:
b"**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
As discussed in https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/issues/1337#issuecomment-900664330 the FAISS document store should save it's configuration when the index is stored on disk. Otherwise, an end-user will have to store the config somewhere else or they'll have to remember the configuration. Also, the `load` method currently does not take any configuration options which means that indexes loaded from disk will always use the default configuration.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
When calling the `save` method a json (?) file is saved which contains the current configuration of the index. The load method will automatically look for a config-file which is located in the same directory as the index file. If a config file is missing, the index will be initialized with the default config (thus keeping backwards compatibility).

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
None"

Title: b'can haystack support Python3.7.6, PyTorch1.9 and CUDA11.1?'
Body:
b'**Question**
can haystack support Python3.7.6, PyTorch1.9 and CUDA11.1?
**Additional context**
I have python 3.7.6 virtual environment installed with anaconda, PyTorch 1.9 installed with CUDA11.1, also transformers 4.10.0, however, when i use the following command to install the Haystack, my PyTorch version was rolled back to PyTorch1.8.1 and CUDA10.2. 
so several questions:
1. how can i make use of my PyTorch version and Cuda version to run Haystack? is it possible?
2. if the answer to question 1 is No, then does it mean that i cannot run Haystack on my RTX3090 because RTX3090 does not support CUDA10.2 (if i am not wrong?)

**FAQ Check**
- [ ] Have you had a look at [our new FAQ page](https://haystack.deepset.ai/overview/faq)?
'

Title: b'julian-risch'
Body:
b"Hi @XingYiBao I added an answer to that question on stack overflow: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/69006922/using-rtx3090-with-haystack Let me copy it here. In short: As of today, the latest haystack release does not support torch 1.9 but the next release will do that. If you don't want to wait two to three weeks, you can use the latest master branch of haystack and FARM as described below.

I have torch 1.9.0 installed with CUDA 11.2 installed and it works fine with the master branches of FARM and haystack. Let me walk you through the steps how to get there.

The problem is that the latest release of haystack 0.9.0 has FARM 0.8.0 as dependency, which fixes the torch dependency to <1.9. However, if you install haystack from its master branch you could remove the fixed FARM 0.8.0 dependency and install FARM from its master branch as well. On the current master branch of FARM, the torch dependency is relaxed to <1.10.

I have in mind the following steps to first install FARM and then haystack from their master branches:
```
  git clone https://github.com/deepset-ai/FARM.git
  cd FARM
  pip install -r requirements.txt
  pip install --editable .
  cd ..
  git clone https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack.git
  cd haystack

  #now edit requirements.txt and remove line with farm==0.8.0

  pip install --editable .
```
Note that all of this wont be necessary when the 1.0.0 version of haystack is released, which will be within the next 3 weeks in late September 2021. Maybe there will also be a minor 0.9.1 even before that, which should solve your problem so that you can simply use `pip install farm-haystack`."

farm-haystack                     0.9.0          /Users/julian/deepset/dev/haystack
```
If you are certain that the installation worked, maybe for some reason you are using a different python version or different virtual environment for running tutorial3. For example, maybe you have python2 and python3 installed and they are somehow mixed up."

Title: b'julian-risch'
Body:

Title: b'Rasa Integration'

b'**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

One of the typical use cases that we saw in the community is using Haystack to boost conversational assistants / chat bots on the long tail of queries. As you can't think of all possible intents beforehand, a QA model is a powerful option to cover unforeseen "information queries". 

The integration of Haystack with the existing conversational frameworks today requires still a lot of manual effort and implementation work. 

**Describe the solution you'd like**

From what I see, Rasa support extern "action servers" that can execute custom code and get triggered via an REST API.

Let's build a "Haystack Action Server", that gets a query and returns answers or documents. 
From what I see, we only need to comply with this API spec: https://rasa.com/docs/action-server/http-api-spec

More info about the Action Servers: https://rasa.com/docs/action-server/actions

Contributions welcome :) '

Title: b'tomgun132'
Body:
b'Hello, I want to comment on some things here.

First, what @prasunanand do is to replace the endpoint of supposedly action server to be the endpoint created by `app.py`. There might be problem when you want to create other custom action other than Haystack since all output from Rasa will be sent to the custom `app.py` instead of custom Rasa action server which can handle the output data from `rasa shell`.

what we can do is to run 3 processes at the same time, `rasa shell` or `rasa run` to start up Rasa server, `rasa run actions` to run Rasa action server, and `python app.py` (Or from [Haystack REST API](https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/master/rest_api/controller/search.py#L186)) to run Haystack app.

> We will need to parse the question from the rasa request [here](https://github.com/prasunanand/haystack-action-server/blob/master/app.py#L25)
> We should probably name the endpoint "rasa-query" add it to our main REST API in haystack ([here](https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/master/rest_api/controller/search.py#L186)).

In my opinion, the better way to do this is to send the request from [here](https://github.com/prasunanand/haystack-action-server/blob/master/actions/actions.py#L21). I think you can access the input text from `tracker.latest_message`

> Not sure if there's anything similar to filters that could be send from rasa to narrow down the search space. Probably not 

As far as I know after reading Rasa's code, I don't think so.

> How is the action triggered? @tomgun132 mentioned that there is a "Fallback" trigger that could be helpful in addition to a specific intent.

The action is triggered when there is [a rule](https://rasa.com/docs/rasa/rules) that define a certain intent will trigger a certain action. The trigger can also be defined in [Stories](https://rasa.com/docs/rasa/writing-stories) as well, but that requires you to create a conversation flow for your chatbot. The "Fallback" trigger is when the Rasa NLU Classifier and/or Core story prediction confidence is below a certain threshold.

> How much further can we simplify action-server.yml (e.g. are all the components like ButtonResponse etc. needed?)

In my own implementation, I'm not using `action-server.yml`, but all the output components like ButtonResponse etc is optional depend on [where you will send the output](https://rasa.com/docs/rasa/messaging-and-voice-channels).

Another way to integrate Haystack to Rasa is to have the Haystack model inside [Rasa Custom Components](https://rasa.com/docs/rasa/2.0.x/components#custom-components). In faq, Rasa has already [built-in FAQ model](https://rasa.com/docs/rasa/chitchat-faqs) if the training data exists. I think this is similar to [this tutorial](https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/master/tutorials/Tutorial4_FAQ_style_QA.ipynb)'

Sorry for my late reply here. I was offline for a while as I recently became a dad and the "onboarding" of my son kept me busy. 

It's really great to see so many people suggesting ideas here! Let's try to bring them together and proceed together on the actual implementation.

I'd prefer having a single API that also contains the Rasa endpoint. However, I'd suggest a separate folder (e.g. "integrations > rasa") or a tutorial, where we showcase how the integration on the rasa side looks like (fallback intent + routing the request to Haystack).   

## Next steps

I think we should start a draft PR and collaborate there. Would be great if we can have one person in charge here for creating the first draft. Then all others can review and suggest improvements.

Title: b'Refactor how args are passed between pipeline nodes (First design)'
Body:
b'As of now:
- we pass a big dictionary from node to node
- each node picks the args defined in its `run()` method
- the rest goes to kwargs
- some nodes also access kwargs for further optional input during `run()`
- everything else is kept in kwargs and in the end the node combines it's own output with the content of kwargs and passes it on to the next node

Problems: 
- Not easy to understand for new users
- Not easy to validate if a pipeline is "acceptable" as there are no standardized input/output types
- Cumbersome arg naming if two nodes use the same parameter name (e.g. `top_k` => we use now a workaround like `top_k_retriever`)
- Unused/ invalid args are silently swallowed while the user might think that they are actually used '

Title: b'oryx1729'
Body:
b'# High-level API design

## `Pipeline.run()` method

a) `pipe.run(query="something", top_k=10, filters={...}, ...)`  these args are global and will be passed to all nodes
b) `pipe.run(query={"retriever_a:": "something"}, top_k={"retriever_a": 10, "reader": 20} labels={"evalnode_a": ...})`  If you want to direct an argument to a specific node only

 Pro: very easy user interface + easy to explain; Con: We don't know about swallowed args

## Passing data between nodes

Passing one big `typeddict` / `dataclass` / `BaseModel` from node to node (similar to Request model in REST API)? 

```python
{
     "documents": List[Document],
     "query": Query,
     "answers": List[Answer],
     "labels": None,
     "params": {"node_abc": {"top_k": 10}, "node_2": {"top_k": 10}, },
     "_debug / meta": {"node_abc": {"documents": List[Document]}
}

    // add "origin_node" field to Document, Answer etc?
    // a) "origin_node": ["dpr", "ranker"]   ["elastic", "ranker"]
    // b) Answer._score_debug = [{"ElasticRetriever": {"bm25-score": 10,
    															{"FARMreader": {"answer-score": 20}}}]


# Implement a input parser in base component that does parameter 
# validations based on correponding component's `run()` signature.
def parse_input(Request):
    node.run(request** + request[params]**)
   
```

### Goals for input parsing

- pass the "main args" to run() (ideally in a way that allows type checking pre runtime?)
- put the "unused main args" in kwargs
- pass _debug
- pass the params for this particular node to run() (we can't check typing here pre-runtime)
- JoinNodes: add "inputs" to method signature instead of accessing kwargs for it

# Pipeline configuration
- pipeline type should be rather "Base" or "Ray"
    - based on root node you can switch behaviour ("file"  indexing, "query"  Query)
    - add helper method `get_input_type()`
- Maybe a third pipeline use case with root node "Labels" for evaluation'

b"The `print_documents()` method assumes that the `meta` field contains the document's name in the field `name`. When documents are added to the document store, we typically add a name to the document. For example, here is a line of code that does that in Tutorial 1:
https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/1c8a03aaa2228006665d7b19476e300e99982878/haystack/preprocessor/utils.py#L267

Title: b'julian-risch'
Body: b'Wow, that\'s a lot of progress in such a short time, great! Regarding the metric: nDCG is typically used if there are continuous relevance scores instead of binary relevance scores given by ground truth labels. For example, filter_1 has a relevance of 3 given query_x, and filter_2 has a relevance of 2 given query_x. In the blogpost that you shared, they have access to "facet clicks for 10,000 most popular queries", which means the can have such continuous relevance scores. Given a query, the relevance of a facet could be the number of people that clicked on it.\r\nSecond, nDCG takes into account the position (rank) of the correct prediction within the sorted list of the predictions by a model. For example, having the correct prediction at the top position (rank) gives a higher nDCG score than having it at the second position (rank).\r\nIn my opinion, accuracy (recall@k) is a good metric for our use case and definitely not wrong. We most likely don\'t have continuous relevance scores available and if we show the top k predictions to the user, it doesn\'t make a big difference whether the correct prediction is at position 1 or 2. '

Title: b'Non-RAG model as Generator for "Generative Q&A with RAG"'
Body:
b'About the tutorial ["Generative QA with "Retrieval-Augmented Generation"](https://haystack.deepset.ai/docs/latest/tutorial7md), is there a way to use a non-RAG model as generator? 

E.g. I would like to use a custom mBART.

For instance, using "facebook/bart-base" in the generator
```
retriever = DensePassageRetriever(
    document_store=document_store,
    query_embedding_model="voidful/dpr-question_encoder-bert-base-multilingual",
    passage_embedding_model="voidful/dpr-ctx_encoder-bert-base-multilingual",
    use_gpu=True,
    embed_title=True,
)

generator = RAGenerator(
    model_name_or_path="facebook/bart-base",
    use_gpu=True,
    top_k=1,
    max_length=200,
    min_length=2,
    embed_title=True,
    num_beams=2,
)
```
raises an error: 
`You are using a model of type bart to instantiate a model of type rag. This is not supported for all configurations of models and can yield errors.`
`AssertionError: Config has to be initialized with question_encoder and generator config`.

I don't understand why do I need to put a RAG model in here if RAG is basically a Retriever (DPR) + Generator (BART). Shouldn't I be able to just put the generator since the retriever is already defined?'

Title: b'julian-risch'
Body:
b'Hi @gianlucabusatta the warning and the error message that you report are raised by the underlying transformers library when `RAGenerator` tries to load `"facebook/bart-base"` as a RAG model: https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/76c4d8bf26de3e4ab23b8afeed68479c2bbd9cbd/src/transformers/models/rag/configuration_rag.py#L132
As the error message states, the model cannot be loaded because it does not provide a question_encoder (among other things).
For `"facebook/bart-base"`, there is actually a different class called `MBartForConditionalGeneration ` in [transformers](https://huggingface.co/transformers/model_doc/mbart.html).

The implementation in haystack is fixed to RAG models and the model `"facebook/rag-token-nq"` used in the tutorial indicates `RagTokenForGeneration` architecture in its [config file](https://huggingface.co/facebook/rag-token-nq/blob/main/config.json). In contrast to that, `"facebook/bart-base"` indicates a `BartModel` architecture in its [config file](https://huggingface.co/facebook/bart-base/blob/main/config.json).'

Title: b'julian-risch'
Body: b"Transformers' RagTokenForGeneration can be initialized with a retriever or a separate retriever can be used which forwards retrieved documents to the RAG model. Here is the documentation page: https://huggingface.co/transformers/model_doc/rag.html\r\nThe generator within transformers' RAG model could be set to a BartForConditionalGeneration model, which is what you would like to do, I think: https://huggingface.co/transformers/model_doc/rag.html#ragmodel\r\nMaybe @lalitpagaria can explain it better?"

Title: b'julian-risch'

Title: b'Extract passage headers during processing of PDF documents'
Body:
b'### What to do
When converting PDF documents to txt with either apache tika or pdf2text we have some functionality to split the documents by passages afterwards. It would be beneficial to have per passage meta information about the title of the pdf document and the (sub)header of the corresponding passage.

### Use-case
This information might be very useful for DPR based retrieval or more rule based retrieval. Rule based retrieval on sub(header) information could be relevant if we can heavily rely on the header information containing specific keywords.
'

Title: b'Extractive QA may not work well enough for FAQ documents'
Body:
b'I have a question.
How your framework will support FAQ document where the answer is not a fact inside of the text but a kind of "recipe" of a solution. For example, for the content of the car manuals or any other FAQ documents. When there is not much word overlap between the question and the answer and extractive QA will not work well enough.

'

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b'Hey @vladgets , 

Can you maybe give an example of such a document + question that you have in mind? 

If I understood you correctly, I see two main directions for your case:
 
### 1) You really have an "FAQ" document with Question + (long) Answers.
In that case, you can try to match a new user question with one in the FAQ document via a Retriever and return the associated "FAQ answer" to the user. In most cases, dense Retrievers work a bit better here as they don't rely on word overlap. In some domains, mixing dense and sparse Retrievers can also be helpful and has become possible in Haystack just recently (https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/issues/125#issuecomment-733646564).
The disadvantage here is that you need a big set of FAQs, and potentially need to fine-tune the Retriever to your own domain.
 
You can give it a try in our Tutorial 4 (in [docs](https://haystack.deepset.ai/docs/latest/tutorial4md) or [colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/master/tutorials/Tutorial4_Tutorial4_FAQ_style_QA.ipynb)). Just be aware that we are currently refactoring this part in Haystack and we will have a slightly different FAQ Pipeline soon. 

### 2) Using extractive / generative QA 
 
If you have regular texts, but no "factoid questions", it really depends on the details here. Modern QA models can do quite more than just extracting small facts. For example, we use them in a financial domain where analysts ask rather open questions like "What is the strategy on ABC?" or "What is the outlook for ABC?". Even "off-the-shelf" models usually find the right passages and return meaningful answers. If you want to improve this further, you can fine-tune the model a bit more on these type of questions - either by creating a manual set of labels via our [annotation tool ](https://haystack.deepset.ai/docs/latest/annotationmd)or using the [user feedback](https://haystack.deepset.ai/docs/latest/domain_adaptationmd#User-Feedback) function. 

Extractive QA has however limitations when the answer is scattered across multiple passages or needs a further "abstraction layer". In that case, you probably need generative QA (see [RAG](https://haystack.deepset.ai/docs/latest/generatormd) in Haystack) or) multi-hop QA (not yet in Haystack, but planned for next year).

Hope this helps! Happy to go into more details, when I understand your use case a bit better...
'

Title: b'delete a document already embedded in Haystack'
Body:
b'I use your haystack to answer the question through the document. During use I have the problem that I can only delete all the embedded vectors of the document when I want to delete it, but not a single document.
I have a temporary solution for those who need it and hope your team can improve it after this time! Here I use Milvus as document store along with SQLite3 for text mapping

`milvus.py`
```
def delete_embedding(self, documents: Union[List[dict], List[Document]], index: Optional[str] = None,
                      batch_size: int = 10_000):
      """
      Delete a document in the DocumentStore.

      :param documents: List of `Dicts` or List of `Documents`. If they already contain the embeddings, we'll index
                                them right away in Milvus. If not, you can later call update_embeddings() to create & index them.
      :param index: (SQL) index name for storing the docs and metadata
      :param batch_size: When working with large number of documents, batching can help reduce memory footprint.
      :raises DuplicateDocumentError: Exception trigger on duplicate document
      :return:
      """
      index = index or self.index
      if len(documents) == 0:
          logger.warning("Calling DocumentStore.write_documents() with empty list")
          return

      document_objects = [Document.from_dict(d) if isinstance(d, dict) else d for d in documents]
      if len(self._get_duplicate_documents(document_objects)) > 0:
          batched_documents = get_batches_from_generator(document_objects, batch_size)
          with tqdm(total=len(document_objects), disable=not self.progress_bar) as progress_bar:
              for document_batch in batched_documents:
                  doc_ids = []
                  for doc in document_batch:
                      doc_ids.append(doc.id)
                  existing_docs = super().get_documents_by_id(ids=doc_ids, index=index)
                  status = self._delete_vector_ids_from_milvus(documents=existing_docs, index=index)
              self.delete_embedding_sql(document_objects)
              progress_bar.update(batch_size)
          progress_bar.close()
      
          self.milvus_server.flush([index])
          status = self.milvus_server.compact(collection_name=index) 
          if status.code != Status.SUCCESS:
              raise RuntimeError(f'Index delete on Milvus server failed: {status}')
      else:
          print("The document is not embedded please try again")
        
def check_exist_document_embedding(self, documents: Union[List[dict], List[Document]]):
    if len(documents) == 0:
        logger.warning("Calling DocumentStore.write_documents() with empty list")
        return

    document_objects = [Document.from_dict(d) if isinstance(d, dict) else d for d in documents]
    if len(self._get_duplicate_documents(document_objects))>0:
        return True
    return False
```
`base.py`
```
def _get_duplicate_documents(self, documents: List[Document]):
        """
        :return: A list of ID Document contain Database.
       """
        documents = self._drop_duplicate_documents(documents)
        documents_found = self.get_documents_by_id(ids=[doc.id for doc in documents], index=self.index)
        ids_exist_in_db = [doc.id for doc in documents_found]
        
        return ids_exist_in_db
```
`sql.py`
```
def delete_embedding_sql(self, documents: Union[List[dict], List[Document]], index: Optional[str] = None,
                        batch_size: int = 10_000,):
        """
        Indexes documents for later queries.

        :param documents: a list of Python dictionaries or a list of Haystack Document objects.
                          For documents as dictionaries, the format is {"text": "<the-actual-text>"}.
                          Optionally: Include meta data via {"text": "<the-actual-text>",
                          "meta":{"name": "<some-document-name>, "author": "somebody", ...}}
                          It can be used for filtering and is accessible in the responses of the Finder.
        :param index: add an optional index attribute to documents. It can be later used for filtering. For instance,
                      documents for evaluation can be indexed in a separate index than the documents for search.
        :param batch_size: When working with large number of documents, batching can help reduce memory footprint.

        :return: None
        """

        index = index or self.index
        if len(documents) == 0:
            return
            
        document_objects = documents
        for i in range(0, len(document_objects), batch_size):
            for doc in document_objects[i: i + batch_size]:
                self.session.query(MetaORM).filter_by(document_id=doc.id).delete()
                self.session.query(DocumentORM).filter_by(id=doc.id).delete()
            try:
                self.session.commit()
            except Exception as ex:
                logger.error(f"Transaction rollback: {ex.__cause__}")
                # Rollback is important here otherwise self.session will be in inconsistent state and next call will fail
                self.session.rollback()
                raise ex
```
'

Title: b'oryx1729'

b'Hi @akkefa, apologies for the delay in getting back.

I had a quick look into [Ray Serve](https://docs.ray.io/en/master/serve/index.html#) for deploying a Pipeline as a distributed graph of components, wherein, each component can be running on a different machine(or on the same machine for development). For instance, a Pipeline can have the retriever running on a CPU machine, while the reader running on a GPU machine. This would allow independently scaling the number of replicas for each component.

Ray Serve can wrap the Haystack components into nodes that could be then be [called](https://docs.ray.io/en/master/serve/http-servehandle.html) with REST APIs or Python interface. This "RayPipeline" instance can then be deployed as an independent Haystack API or integrated with existing APIs of external systems. From a high level, the approach sounds reasonable given each Haystack Component is independent and can interact using APIs.

An open question is to understand if using the low-level [Ray Core](https://docs.ray.io/en/master/walkthrough.html#) instead of [Ray Serve](https://docs.ray.io/en/master/serve/index.html) would have any advantages and how complex the implementation would be? 



'

Title: b'Drop score field from answers to prevent confusion with probability/confidence'
Body:
b'Answers contain two fields `score` and `probability`, where `probability` is the confidence score calculated and optionally calibrated in FARM. `probability` takes into account only the start index of the answer but is guaranteed to be in range 0 to 1. `score` was previously used as confidence score and has no upper range limitation. It has no advantage over `probability` except for taking into account both start index and end index. 
```
{'answer': 'Eddard',
 'context': 's Nymeria after a legendary warrior queen. '
            'She travels with her father, Eddard, to '
            "King's Landing when he is made Hand of the "
            'King. Before she leaves,',
 'document_id': 'ba2a8e87ddd95e380bec55983ee7d55f',
 'meta': {'name': '43_Arya_Stark.txt'},
 'offset_end': 78,
 'offset_end_in_doc': 153,
 'offset_start': 72,
 'offset_start_in_doc': 147,
 'probability': 0.9899835586547852,
 'score': 15.927592277526855}
```

I see two tasks:
* 'score' should be dropped from answers as it creates confusion between `probability`, `confidence`, and `score` (for example see https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/issues/1219).
* Documentation needs to be updated. It currently lists a field called `confidence, which does not exist: https://haystack.deepset.ai/docs/latest/readermd#Confidence-Scores

Make sure Documents and Answers throughout Haystack all return the same variable `(relevance) score` (or named differently). With a fixed range of 0 to 1 if possible.

Related issue in FARM: https://github.com/deepset-ai/FARM/issues/808'

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b"I am pretty confident that this is not related to haystack's `update_embeddings` but rather your FAISS index growing out of RAM. 
See:
- https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/issues/758
- https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/issues/1326

Possible workarounds: 
- increase RAM of your server
- move to another docstore that e.g. allows simpler distribution across machines ( milvus, opensearch ...)
- compress your index in FAISS, see also https://github.com/facebookresearch/faiss/wiki/Indexes-that-do-not-fit-in-RAM"

Title: b'Semantic Answer similarity evaluation'
Body:
b'Common metrics for evaluating QA like Exact Match or f1 score are very strict. They can be better applied to settings where an exact entity (name, date or number) needs to be extracted.
For more complex answers we want a more loose evaluation.

Inspired by other domains like machine translation we have started experiments with a semantic textual similarity metric between ground truth answer and predicted answer in https://github.com/deepset-ai/FARM/pull/803

We now want to bring this functionality to Haystack.

Prioritize pipeline eval.
'

Title: b'Add user feedback buttons to UI to collect domain-specifc training data'
Body:
b'**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
If you work on domain corpora, collecting additional training data to improve your reader or retriever models is very helpful. 
For collecting training data, there are two main options: 
a) Manual Labelling
b) User feedback for "live predictions" 

b) is particularly promising if you don't have enough time or resources for a) OR if you want to continuously improve your model once it is production. 

We already have the API for storing user feedback and used it successfully in some deployments. In these deployments, we used proprietary user interfaces to collect feedback. Let's add those feedback buttons also to our Haystack Demo UI based on streamlit so that everybody can experiment with it more easily and understand the mechanics.

- Add :+1: / :-1: buttons in the streamlit UI that allow capturing user feedback per result

Title: b'PiffPaffM'
Body:
b'@lalitpagaria: Thanks for the input. I started to try the various options. Here a quick summary of my initial findings:

Vulnerability Checks:

- **Bandit** is a very cool tool and we should test it in more detail in the future, but it is not really the solution we are looking for. It analysis the code regarding common security issues. We want to scan for CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures). This means that we want to scan for publicly known information-security vulnerabilities in publicly released software packages.

- **Safety** is a tool used for finding vulnerabilities. That is what we want to do and it is working pretty well. 
Cons: The underlying vulnerability database on which this tool is based is updated monthly. However, in order to get access to a complete vulnerability database you need to buy a [subscription plan](https://pyup.io/pricing/). 
Pros: It comes with a deep GitHub integration: https://pyup.io/safety/ci/.

- **Snyk**: I have not checked it in detail but it is quite costly compared to Saftey

- **Guardrails**: Looks promising as well. They just come as Github App. I have not tested it so far.

- We also need to scan our docker containers. It is not enough to scan the dependencies as we have to make sure that we use the latest stable version here. A lot of vulnerabilities are caused by older ubuntu versions.

License compliance:

- **pip-licenses** to be checked
- **liccheck** to be checked
- **license-finder** to be checked (looks promising and is used by GitLab https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/user/compliance/license_compliance/; https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/security-products/analyzers/license-finder)

Next steps:
- Test tools
- Benchmarking 
'

Title: b'Merge behavior of multiple search requests in pipeline.py'

Currently, the merge functionality mostly supports the weighted average of scores of multiple retrievers. One of the issues is each retriever throws a different set of candidates. In most cases, the candidate documents are not overlapping across multiple retrievers which forces the weighted average to be lower than the ideal desired weighted average if the actual scores were considered. This has the unwanted side effect of not having the contribution from all retrievers 

File path: https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/master/haystack/pipeline.py

A potential solution would be to get the candidate scores for the union of all unique documents across all retrievers. This will ensure that the weighted average of scores makes sense.

No. Above approach itself minimizes the unwanted side effects of top n candidates from each retrievers



"

Title: b'cvgoudar'
Body: b"Merging scores where they are not normalized to a scale doesn't work. One possible option is to normalize (optional parameter) by the highest score value of each retriever and then do weighted average could be a solution. Secondly for cases where the score is expected to be between 0-1 (for ex: cosine similarity) we can use them as-is. Also, the scores from dot_products have significant variation even for embedding retriever models as well.\r\n\r\nIn our setup we tried weighted averaging of only cosine similarity scores. The second observation was weighted averaging also may not be ideal solution. Usually when one of the scores is really high it may be the best match. However weighted averaging may dilute the effect. For best match there may be need for giving boost to max score (normalized variant or common scale) across retrievers."

Title: b'lalitpagaria'
Body:
b'@Timoeller and @cvgoudar How about adding `PostProcessing` Node? Which is kind of `JoinNode` but more related to prediction part.
We have recently added it in Obsei (thanks to @akar5h contribution), which perform [`Inference Aggregation`](https://github.com/obsei/obsei/blob/master/obsei/postprocessor/inference_aggregator.py). User can supply function (or choose from pre-existing one like weightage avg or max voting etc) based on which aggregation needs to be performed. Currently our pipeline looks like this, I think some pieces make sense to Haystack as well -
```
Observer -> PreProcessor (TextCleaner and TextSplitter) -> Analyzer -> PostProcessor (InferenceAggregator) -> Informer
```'

Title: b'Leading space in answers since haykstack 0.9.0'

b"**Question**
After updating haystack from version 0.8.0 to 0.9.0, I'm noticing a leading space with each answer coming out of the TransformersReader. I'm trying to understand where they come from and how to properly remove them.

My pipeline consists in an ElasticsearchRetriever with an ElasticsearchDocumentStore and a TransformersReader with a RoBERTa based model (camembert) and the associated tokenizer.

I've read a number of things related to the handling of spaces but they don't seem to be responsible for what I'm observing:
- there is this change #1121 in the preprocessor, but I'm not using any preprocessor,
- I understant that RoBERTa treats space as part of the token and it's tokenizer requires a space before each token. This could explain why we're getting spaces as output of the pipeline. There is a discussion an a number of issues about it in the transformers repository (https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues/1196) but the issue and related commit are dated before haystack version 0.8.0, thus they don't explain why I'm observing this change now.

Is there a particular option in the TransformersReader or elsewhere in the pipeline that I'm missing?


**FAQ Check**
- [X] Have you had a look at [our new FAQ page](https://haystack.deepset.ai/docs/latest/faqmd)?
"

Title: b'Timoeller'
Body:
b'REALM and ORQA are of course very influential papers in our domain and we liked the idea of joint end-to-end training of retriever and reader. Pretraining seems to improve  zero shot recall for the retriever (See REAM ablation studies, table 2, row 2). This is of course very interesting when you want to develop retrievers that work on out of domain data (or even other languages) like we do.
The actual engineering to do the training, especially creation and periodic updating of the document index for getting a training signal seems amazing, yet rather complex. I doubt we can get the training part into pytorch or haystack quickly.

 -------

We also see the retriever part of these papers similar to DPR and are interested in getting this into haystack. It seems as if the pretrained retriever weights (QueryEmbedder and DocumentEmbedder) could be easily plugged into the existing DPR code (we are currently changing from fb dpr code to HF dpr code in #308). We would only need conversion of tf Bert models to pytorch + add the last linear down projecting layer.
My speculation of what the data in the GCP bucket (linked on REALM github) is:
- cc_news_pretrained/embedder/ are the retriever files
- cc_news_pretrained/embedder/saved_model.pb should be the pretrained downprojecting layers for question and document retrievers because the file is just 46MB large. 
- I only see one /realm-data/cc_news_pretrained/embedder/variables/variables.data-00000-of-00001 of size 420MB, which seems like the BERT they use as base encoder model. So since there is only one BERT model I believe they use tied weights for query and document embedder? From a quick scan of the papers I could not verify this hypothesis...

 -------

@antoniolanza1996 do you see it the same way or have other opinions, especially about the model files and conversion strategy? Would you like to work on this with out support?'

Title: b'antoniolanza1996'
Body:
b'Hi @Timoeller,
thanks for considering this enhancement.

I totally agree with you on the training part. It could be really complex to integrate on the current Haystack version.

However, I also thought, like you, of something similar to DPR implementation. In particular, we can consider the retriever part composed by a `BiEncoder` (i.e. question encoder and document encoder). With this "abstraction", if one wants to use DPR as retriever component, he/she could use something similar to: 
`biencoder = BiEncoder(question_encoder="dpr-question_encoder-single-nq-base", document_encoder="dpr-ctx_encoder-single-nq-base") `
Instead, if one wants to use ORQA:
`biencoder = BiEncoder(question_encoder="orqa-question_encoder", document_encoder="orqa-document_encoder") `
Similarly, for REALM: 
`biencoder = BiEncoder(question_encoder="realm-question_encoder", document_encoder="realm-document_encoder") `

If the models will be uploaded in HF, there will be no problems to quickly integrate ORQA e REALM in Haystack. In my main comment I have cited two HF issues which ask for models addition, however I don't know if someone will take them into account (I hope so).

Meanwhile, I have read ORQA and REALM code and I have come up with this speculations:
1. Files under `realm-data/cc_news_pretrained/` are outputs of pre-training step. In particular, starting from ICT pre-trained model (introduced in ORQA paper), they apply the REALM pre-training and obtain 2 embedder models (1 for retrieval (i.e. `realm-data/cc_news_pretrained/embedder/`) and 1 for answer extraction (i.e. `realm-data/cc_news_pretrained/bert/`)).
2. At this point, I asked myself (and I noted that you had my same doubt) `question encoder == document encoder`? I have better investigated and I have also talked with one of the papers authors to understand something more. He said to me that, _at the end of pre-training_, indeed they are the same! 
However, after pre-training, we have to perform document indexing (thus using `realm-data/cc_news_pretrained/embedder/`) and then fine-tuning. During fine-tuning, document encoder is not considered (clearly because all the documents have been already indexed). But the question encoder (together with reader encoder) is trained. Thus, weights between document encoder (i.e. `realm-data/cc_news_pretrained/embedder/`) and question encoder (i.e. fine-training retriever output) may change. Indeed for this reason we can state that `question encoder != document encoder`.
3. Where should we find the question encoder and reader encoder? We have to see at the end of fine-tuning step (i.e. after [orqa_experiment.py](https://github.com/google-research/language/blob/394675a831ae45ea434abb50655e7975c68a7121/language/orqa/experiments/orqa_experiment.py) run). Here, TensorFlow saves both the models in one checkpoint **(+++)**.

Thus, after this long (and boring) comment, I think that:
1. REALM document encoder could be downloaded from `realm-data/cc_news_pretrained/embedder/`
2. REALM question encoder and REALM reader encoder should be extracted from `realm-data/orqa_nq_model_from_realm/export/best_default/checkpoint/` (or `realm-data/orqa_wq_model_from_realm/export/best_default/checkpoint/` if we want the models fine-tuned on WebQuestions dataset).

Hope it helps. I will wait for your reply.




**(+++)** To confirm that TensorFlow saves both the models in one checkpoint, please consider authors example on NQ dataset. Their best checkpoint is stored in `realm-data/orqa_nq_model_from_realm/export/best_default/checkpoint/`. In terms of storage, this directory is approximately **6x** `realm-data/cc_news_pretrained/embedder` (clearly don't consider `realm-data/cc_news_pretrained/embedder/encoded/` which contains document embeddings). According to this [issue](https://github.com/google-research/bert/issues/63), all it makes sense (indeed **3x** for BERT question encoded + **3x** for BERT reader encoder), thus in this checkpoint there are 2 BERT models.'

Title: b'antoniolanza1996'
Body:
b'Hi @Timoeller,
I will try to better explain my findings. 

> This I do not understand, since they have engineered this update-able index. Why not update the index for finetuning, too, to jointly train question AND document embedder.

The update-able index is only used during pre-training. Indeed, the main goal of REALM paper is to introduce an outstanding pre-training step.

However, when the model should be fine-tuned for the task of Open-domain Question Answering, they states [here](https://github.com/google-research/language/tree/master/language/realm#code) that we have to use ORQA codebase.
According to [ORQA README](https://github.com/google-research/language/tree/master/language/orqa#fine-tuning), we have to run an orqa_experiment and this experiment uses [orqa_model.py](https://github.com/google-research/language/blob/master/language/orqa/models/orqa_model.py).
Reading this code you can see that question embedder is initialised [here](https://github.com/google-research/language/blob/master/language/orqa/models/orqa_model.py#L109) using the BERT model stored after pre-training. Hence, during fine-tuning, its parameters could be _fine-tuned_ accordingly. 
However, there is no document embedder loaded similarly to question embedder. Only [here](https://github.com/google-research/language/blob/master/language/orqa/models/orqa_model.py#L116) a ScaNN searcher is loaded. It contains the already indexed documents (i.e. document embeddings). This means that the document embedder will not fine-tuned (because they suppose that ALL the documents have already been indexed in ScaNN). 

I have also found this comment in _section 2.3_ of this [new paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2007.00814.pdf):
> "After pretraining, both ORQA and REALM freeze the passages index and encoder and subsequently fine-tune the question encoder to retrieve passages whose content helps a jointly-trained reader model extract the correct answer"

The meaning of this quoted sentence is really similar to what I have tried to explain.

Are you agree with me or is there something wrong?'

All right, it makes sense.

> Are you actively working on this? 

No, I have postponed this work as it is not strictly imminent to implement for my thesis. I will consider it in the coming weeks.
'

Title: b'antoniolanza1996'
Body:
b'I have never seen Poly-Encoders before but, after a first glance, I agree with you. Indeed, the main idea is similar. 

As you said, ColBERT is really interesting. But, I think, it is more computational intensive compared to other dense approaches (e.g. DPR, ORQA, REALM) at inference time. Indeed, ColBERT requires a lot of memory and more math operations to compute MaxSim.
As a simple example: 
For a single document, ORQA/REALM saves one 128-dim vector and DPR saves one 768-dim vector. Instead, ColBERT should save 120-150 128-dim vectors.
_Note:_ I have written 120-150 because ColBERT authors use the same wiki split as DPR. In this wiki split, each passage contains 100 words. Hence, in average, 100 words are approximately 120-150 tokens with DPRTokenizer.

I think that, after thorough tests, one could state if it is worth the risk. I hope so because the achieved results in the paper are really outstanding.



> More than happy to collaborate to get these features into haystack once your thesis is finished.

As you previously advised, I have converted TF models in PyTorch ones and I have plugged them into DPR implementation. However, I had to use DPRTokenizer. In particular, I have used DPR checkpoint for `query_tokenizer` and `passage_tokenizer` and my converted checkpoint for `query_encoder` and `passage_encoder` (related to these [lines](https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/master/haystack/retriever/dense.py#L83-L87)).

I have tested both ORQA and REALM retriever models and they seems to work. In the coming weeks I'll run more intensive tests and I let you know if there are problems.

If you want, I can share PyTorch converted models, but this is not a real solution, it's just a rough "hack" that I have done to test these trained checkpoints.
Hopefully, models will be published in HF. Hence, we can use them in a BiEncoder abstraction (as previously discussed). 
'
