Title: b'Combination of multiple retrievers'
Body:
b"Originating from a discussion in #104. 

**What**
Combine multiple scores during retrieval (e.g. embeddings similarity of multiple text fields, or BM25 + Embedding similarity ...) 

**Options**

a) Concatenation of Retrievers: Make the Finder accept a list of Retrievers and combine their scores (incl. weights) before feeding results to the Reader
Pro: most generic solution also allowing combination of BM25 + EmbeddingRetriever
Con: Two separate retriever queries (suboptimal efficiency in some cases)

b) New MultiEmbeddingRetriever: Extend the EmbeddingRetriever to the case of multiple Embeddings
Pro: simple implementation without side effects on the regular user interface
Con: won't allow the combination of other retriever methods (e.g. ElasticsearchRetriever + EmbeddingRetriver)

I am leaning towards a), but could see b) as a simpler short-term solution for the original use case discussed in #104 .



Issue is synchronized with this [Jira Task](https://deepset-ai.atlassian.net/browse/HS-42) by [Unito](https://www.unito.io/learn-more)
"

Title: b'tholor'

b'@guillim  Quick update:  We have the first version now implemented and you can use it like this: 

```python
from haystack.pipeline import DocumentSearchPipeline, ExtractiveQAPipeline, Pipeline, JoinDocuments
from haystack.document_store.elasticsearch import ElasticsearchDocumentStore
from haystack.reader.farm import FARMReader
from haystack.retriever.sparse import ElasticsearchRetriever

# Building blocks (= Nodes)
document_store = ElasticsearchDocumentStore(host="localhost", username="", password="", index="document")
es_retriever = ElasticsearchRetriever(document_store=document_store)
reader = FARMReader(model_name_or_path="deepset/roberta-base-squad2", use_gpu=False)
...

# Combine via default pipeline (here: QA)
qa_pipe = ExtractiveQAPipeline(reader=reader, retriever=retriever)
res = qa_pipe.run(question="Who is the father of Sansa Stark?", top_k_retriever=2, top_k_reader=5)
print(res)
qa_pipe.draw()


# Or build your own custom pipeline to model complex search routes (e.g. combine multiple retrievers)
p = Pipeline()
p.add_node(component=es_retriever, name="ESRetriever1", inputs=["Query"])
p.add_node(component=dpr_retriever, name="DPRRetriever1", inputs=["Query"])
p.add_node(component=JoinDocuments(join_mode="concatenate"), name="JoinResults", inputs=["ESRetriever1", "DPRRetriever1"])
```

@tanaysoni We still need to add other options for `join_mode` (e.g. combining doc scores + weighting)'

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b'Ok, you have 3 options to improve: 
1) Smaller reader model. bert-large is a really heavy model. I'd recommend switching to `deepset/roberta-base-squad2` or `deepset/minilm-uncased-squad2`. This should give you a 1.5x speed up. See also the [docs] https://haystack.deepset.ai/en/docs/readermd).
2) Split your texts before adding them to the documentstore. 170k characters is quite a big portion of text for the reader and the time scales linearly with text length. In many scenarios, you can reduce this down to 10-50k characters by a good splitting strategy without any loss in accuracy. In your case this would mean a speed up of 3x-17x . We'll have better built-in options for splitting in Haystack soon (). For now, you could try splitting by "passages" (i.e. text.split("\n\n")) or a fixed number of words. 
3) Move to a GPU. This will give you a 30-45x speed up and is highly recommended for production.

Hope this helps'

Title: b'brandenchan'
Body:
b'Hi @datalee, the `InMemoryDocumentStore` was created as a lightweight prototyping option for those who do not want to install the dependencies required for the other document stores. It is not our most efficient Document Store and sadly there is no save / load feature.

If you are looking for a document store which is faster and scales better, I'd recommend you try the `ElasticsearchDocumentStore` or the `SQLDocumentStore`. 

SQLite is installed by default in many operating systems so you might not have to install anything to make it work already. Elasticsearch needs to be installed and running in the background already but setting it up is as easy as these two lines if you have Docker.

```
docker pull docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch:7.9.2
docker run -d -p 9200:9200 -e "discovery.type=single-node" elasticsearch:7.9.2
```

Another advantage of these two options is that the instances run outside of Haystack. This means that you can index documents using Haystack, and even after your script has finished running, the indexed documents will still be there in the SQL / ES instance. The next time you run the script, you can skip reindexing the same documents.

If you are working with Dense Retrieval methods like DPR or SentenceTransformers, you will want to use a vector optimized Document Store like FAISS or Milvus. 

I hope this helps!'

Title: b'julian-risch'
Body:
b'@UmerTariq1 Thank you for your detailed description of the problem and the notebook. You mention that the result is perfect when you run the code for the first time but duplicates show up when you run it a second time. I think the reason is the following: Although you initialize the ElasticsearchDocumentStore (rerun first 2 lines), the underlying elasticsearch instance is the same. print(f"Document store still contains {document_store.get_document_count()} documents.")

Title: b'julian-risch'

```
document_store = ElasticsearchDocumentStore(host="localhost", username="", password="", index="document") 
document_store.delete_all_documents()
document_store.write_documents(haystackData) 
retriever = ElasticsearchRetriever(document_store=document_store)
```
Note that this deletes all documents in your local elasticsearch instance in the index called "document".
Please let me know if this solves your problem. Thank you.'

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b'Hi @aaronbriel , 

Your are right, that general embedding models like `deepset/sentence_bert` can do a fairly good job across different domains. 
However, we saw that you can still improve model performance by taking such a model and fine-tuning it on domain data.

Minimal example:


```
from haystack import Finder
from haystack.database.memory import InMemoryDocumentStore
from haystack.reader.farm import FARMReader
from haystack.retriever.sparse import TfidfRetriever

READER = FARMReader(model_name_or_path="./model",
                    use_gpu=False,
                    context_window_size=500)

t = """In 2010, Hammond was the president of the 31st Herefordshire Country Fair held at Hampton Court in Hope under Dinmore. His involvement caused unprecedented attendance with nearly 15,000 people drawn to the event to meet the presenter.[73]

In March 2012, Hammond passed his B206 LST helicopter licence and has since owned a Robinson R44 Raven II helicopter.[74]

In September 2018, his wife reported that she and Richard, along with their fifteen-year-old daughter, had been burgled while sleeping."""

document_store = InMemoryDocumentStore()

document_store.write_documents([
    {
        'meta': {'name': 'custom'},
        'text': t

retriever = TfidfRetriever(document_store=document_store)
finder = Finder(READER, retriever)

result = finder.get_answers(

    top_k_retriever=10,

Title: b'Advice regarding normalisation of source texts'
Body:
b'**Question**
Do you have any advice / recommendations regarding normalisation of source texts?

**Additional context**
This came up when I was evaluating the QA capabilities recently - I tried pulling in a bunch of Wikipedia text on the Royal Family and testing it on different kings and queens.  The issue I noticed was that often if the question wasn't made to match the way the monarch's regnal number (ie Henry VIII for "Henry the Eighth") was expressed then it would struggle to zero in on the right person and often ended up giving non-sense answers.

It seems like this is a challenge partly for the retreiver but also partly for the reader.  It's quite common in the royal context I was using for testing, for distinct people to be referenced near each other, eg Henry VII might come up in a piece on Henry VIII and the reader would effectively be blind to the numbers as a way of telling that it was looking at text relating to the right individual unless the question expresses the number in the exact same form in the text.

Is there any advice on best practices here or things you've found to work well / less well?

To be clear I'm not just focused on numeric representations (ie VIII vs 8 vs eighth) but that was one that came up a load in my specific test topic.

Is use of DPR relevant here perhaps? I was thinking that maybe it would help, based on this comment in the Better_Retrieval_via_DPR tutorial:
> Pros: Captures semantinc similarity instead of "word matches" (e.g. **synonyms**, related topics ...)

since it looks like it might figure out synonyms as they'll be used in similar contexts within text and thus it might apply to this kind of problem.

Working effectively with synonyms would be ideal as it would avoid the need to alter the source as much (at all?) and that's a great benefit when the source may have several synonyms for a thing present.

Anyway, would love to hear what you suggest.  I did try searching for this (in the repo and in your docs) but didn't see anything that looked like it answered this (beyond that tutorial possibly).  I hope I haven't overlooked something obvious  

Thanks a lot for this great repo - it's really impressive!'

Title: b'brandenchan'
Body:
b'Hi @nmstoker, what you raise is actually generally quite a tricky issue within NLP but there are different methods of coping with it. 

Yes as you mentioned, I would certainly recommend trying DPR for retrieval! Since it is Transformer based, it relies on its representation of meaning rather than exact string matching. This means that it is more robust to this kind of variation  (e.g. `eighth` vs `8` vs `VIII`). This also applies for all the Reader models that we have which are also transformer based. Try it out and let us know how it goes!

These different forms of the same word are trickier for the Elasticsearch / BM25 retriever which is looking for exact matches of words. One method that we used to help here is to extract aliases and keywords. For example you would create a list which states that `Henry VIII` is an alias of `Henry the Eighth`. If a certain text contains one of these, you add all its aliases as keywords to Elasticsearch alongside the document. When querying, you can configure Elasticsearch to consider any of these aliases a match. These aliases and their extraction from the document need to be done manually but we found that in some domains (e.g. in specific domain wiki corpora) this is quite doable. I hope this helps!'

Title: b'oryx1729'

> Can we insert multiple documents at the same index in a ES Store?

yes, you can call `document_store.write_documents()` with a list of documents you want to add in the index.

> What is the default behaviour when we do store.write_documents(index) to an index which already exists in the store?

The documents would get added to the Elasticsearch index. If there's a clash of document ID with an existing document, it should get overwritten.

-------

Title: b'Timoeller'
Body:
b'Hey @chingfhen thanks for looking into the annotation tool in combination with Haystack. Are you using it to create positive examples then?

----------------

About negative examples in the annotation tool: 
Explicitly creating questions that do not have an answer is not a feature we currently have, but we might be interested in including it.
Though you can create no_answers if you upload pre-defined questions. Then you can mark questions as "Answer is not given" when hovering over the question (there appears a pen symbol to the right). 

 ---------------

About haystack Reader. Yes, the text is split into passages, only the passage contianing the answer is a positive passage, the other passages are marked as negative. You could see them as "soft negative" since they are not explicitly chosen to not contain the answer (they might even contain a valid answer). 
Nevertheless we have seen increased performance scores when adding "soft negative" passages to the training. We are unsure if adding the "soft negatives" increases the generalization of the model (which would be awesome) or simply adjusts to the style of labeling (which would be a form of overfitting).'

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b'Hey @tgalery , 

Super sorry for my late reply here! Your question somehow slipped through as I thought I already posted an answer here. 

Interesting scenario that you have in mind. Limiting the QA Reader to a certain set of documents is definitely possible in Haystack. Here's one way of implementing it: 

```python

from haystack.document_store.elasticsearch import ElasticsearchDocumentStore
from haystack.reader.farm import FARMReader
from haystack.utils import print_answers
from haystack.retriever.sparse import ElasticsearchRetriever
from haystack.pipeline import ExtractiveQAPipeline

# Building blocks
document_store = ElasticsearchDocumentStore(host="localhost", username="", password="", index="document")
retriever = ElasticsearchRetriever(document_store=document_store)
reader = FARMReader(model_name_or_path="deepset/roberta-base-squad2", use_gpu=True)

# Pipeline
pipeline = ExtractiveQAPipeline(reader=reader, retriever=retriever)
predictions = pipeline.run(query="Who is the father of Sansa Stark?", top_k_retriever=3, top_k_reader=5)
print_answers(predictions, details="minimal")


# Get document ids from predictions
doc_ids = [p["document_id"] for p in predictions["answers"]]
# Use them as a filter for the second query
second_preds = pipeline.run(query="Who is enchanted by the knights?", top_k_retriever=3, top_k_reader=5, filters={"_id": doc_ids })

```

Alternatively, if you want to bypass the retriever in the second query, you could also call `reader.predict(query="...", documents= ...)` and pass a list of Documents there (e.g. the ones you retrieved in an earlier query). See this part in the code for details https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/f3a3b73d9b7a0446a17f48dd398449677521eeb9/haystack/reader/farm.py#L333

Let me know if that helps!


> Is it possible to have read only connections to the databases (Elasticsearch and SQL variants) ? It seems we make some PUT requests when we initialise an elastic store

Once your index is initialized you could set `create_index=False` when initializing the `ElasticsearchDocumentstore`. Queries should then still work with a read-only connection. However, bear in mind that adding new docs or updating embeddings (for DPR Retriever) won't work. If you already have an existing, custom elasticsearch index that was not created by Haystack, you can also connect to this one by supplying the appropriate names for `search_fields`, `text_fields` etc in the init of the doc store.

> We doing some basic import of classes , FAISS seems to be loaded (is that the intended behaviour) ?

Yes, the logs that you probably see are ("Loading faiss with AVX2 support.") are created when importing the FAISS library. This happens in various places (e.g. also in Huggingface's transformers + datasets libraries) if FAISS is installed on the system. There's no need to worry about it though. It's not loading any heavy components or indices.'

Title: b'thenewera-ru'
Body:
b"I've tried running the training DPR notebook in Colab having and also got stuck.
The problem is that `calc_chunk_size` that is being used to calculate default `max_chunk_size` doesn't take into account available `RAM`.
```python
def calc_chunksize(num_dicts, min_chunksize=4, max_chunksize=2000, max_processes=128):
    if mp.cpu_count() > 3:
        num_cpus = min(mp.cpu_count() - 1 or 1, max_processes)  # -1 to keep a CPU core free for xxx
    else:
        num_cpus = min(mp.cpu_count(), max_processes) # when there are few cores, we use all of them

    dicts_per_cpu = np.ceil(num_dicts / num_cpus)
    # automatic adjustment of multiprocessing chunksize
    # for small files (containing few dicts) we want small chunksize to ulitize all available cores but never less
    # than 2, because we need it to sample another random sentence in LM finetuning
    # for large files we want to minimize processor spawning without giving too much data to one process, so we
    # clip it at 5k
    multiprocessing_chunk_size = int(np.clip((np.ceil(dicts_per_cpu / 5)), a_min=min_chunksize, a_max=max_chunksize))
    # This lets us avoid cases in lm_finetuning where a chunk only has a single doc and hence cannot pick
    # a valid next sentence substitute from another document
    if num_dicts != 1:
        while num_dicts % multiprocessing_chunk_size == 1:
            multiprocessing_chunk_size -= -1
    dict_batches_to_process = int(num_dicts / multiprocessing_chunk_size)
    num_processes = min(num_cpus, dict_batches_to_process) or 1

    return multiprocessing_chunk_size, num_processes
``` 

I'm assuming not everyone has an opportunity to fine-tune DPR on their own machine with `40+` gb of RAMS. So I suggest to

1. Improve `calc_chunksize` by taking the `RAM` into account.
2. As a quick fix In tutorial - pass manually the `max_chunksize=300` when creating `DataSilo` object.
```python
# 3. Create a DataSilo that loads several datasets (train/dev/test), provides DataLoaders for them and calculates a few descriptive statistics of our datasets
# NOTE: In FARM, the dev set metrics differ from test set metrics in that they are calculated on a token level instead of a word level
data_silo = DataSilo(processor=processor, 
                     batch_size=batch_size, 
                     distributed=distributed,
                     max_multiprocessing_chunksize=300)
```

Let's discuss it here or reopen new issue?"

Title: b'Allow for a custom `tokenizer_class` while loading DPR models'
Body:
b'Hi all!

I just recently re-started my DPR testing with the newest version of haystack (v0.7.0). I use a custom made model which is based on camemBERT (French Roberta). Before, the Tokenizer was working thanks to the nice `farm` tokenizer loading which allows for several types of tokenizers, among them camemBERT tokenizer. 

Unfortunately this is no longer possible because now we fix `tokenizer_class="DPRQuestionEncoderTokenizer"` and `tokenizer_class="DPRContextEncoderTokenizer")` (see here https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/6efa4f06c1476c0cc4ef265d952393a854c119b3/haystack/retriever/dense.py#L111) 

Would it be possible to have an extra parameter in the `DensePassageRetriever` constructor, such as `infer_tokenizer_class=True`? This parameter, if `True`, would set `tokenizer_class` to `None` and thus force the use of `Tokenizer._infer_tokenizer_class` later on. I could propose something similar as PR ofc.

What do you think ?
Thanks !'

Title: b'Semantic search only tutorial'
Body:
b'**Question**
I saw that the tutorials are more for QA systems. Is there also a semantic search tutorial for finding documents based on semantic search (and even better with the aid of sentence transformers)?


'

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b'Hey @gevezex , 

We don't have a dedicated Tutorial for semantic document search. However, it's quite similar to the QA Tutorials with the difference of not using the Reader component. You can use different retrievers (Elasticsearch, DPR, Embedding). In the `EmbeddingRetriever` you can also use sentence-transformers 

Here's a small "recipe" (adjusted from [Tutorial 6](https://haystack.deepset.ai/docs/latest/tutorial6md)): 

```python
from haystack.document_store.faiss import FAISSDocumentStore
from haystack.preprocessor.cleaning import clean_wiki_text
from haystack.preprocessor.utils import convert_files_to_dicts, fetch_archive_from_http
from haystack.retriever.dense import DensePassageRetriever

document_store = FAISSDocumentStore(faiss_index_factory_str="Flat")

# ## Preprocessing of documents
# Let's first get some documents that we want to query
doc_dir = "data/article_txt_got"
s3_url = "https://s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/deepset.ai-farm-qa/datasets/documents/wiki_gameofthrones_txt.zip"
fetch_archive_from_http(url=s3_url, output_dir=doc_dir)

# convert files to dicts containing documents that can be indexed to our datastore
dicts = convert_files_to_dicts(dir_path=doc_dir, clean_func=clean_wiki_text, split_paragraphs=True)

# Now, let's write the docs to our DB.
document_store.write_documents(dicts)

### Retriever

# Recommended: DPR
# retriever = DensePassageRetriever(document_store=document_store,
#                                   query_embedding_model="facebook/dpr-question_encoder-single-nq-base",
#                                   passage_embedding_model="facebook/dpr-ctx_encoder-single-nq-base",
#                                   max_seq_len_query=64,
#                                   max_seq_len_passage=256,
#                                   batch_size=2,
#                                   use_gpu=True,
#                                   embed_title=True,
#                                   use_fast_tokenizers=True
#                                   )

# Alternative: Single encoder for example via sentence transformers
from haystack.retriever.dense import EmbeddingRetriever
retriever = EmbeddingRetriever(document_store=document_store,
                               embedding_model="sentence-transformers/roberta-base-nli-stsb-mean-tokens", # from huggingface's model hub
                               use_gpu=True,
                               model_format="farm", # you can also use "sentence-transformers" here to load the models with the respective framework
                               )


# Important:
# Now that after we have the DPR initialized, we need to call update_embeddings() to iterate over all
# previously indexed documents and update their embedding representation.
# While this can be a time consuming operation (depending on corpus size), it only needs to be done once.
# At query time, we only need to embed the query and compare it the existing doc embeddings which is very fast.
document_store.update_embeddings(retriever)

### Pipeline
# Select the default pipeline for document search or build your own custom one (e.g. combining multiple retrievers).
# See details here: https://haystack.deepset.ai/docs/latest/pipelinesmd
from haystack.pipeline import DocumentSearchPipeline
pipe = DocumentSearchPipeline(retriever=retriever)

## Voil! Ask a question!
prediction = pipe.run(query="Who is the father of Arya Stark?", top_k_retriever=10)
print(prediction)
# Returns list of docs:
# {'query': 'Who is the father of Arya Stark?', 'documents': [
#{'text': '\n===Storylines===\nBrandon "Bran" Stark is the second son and fourth child of Eddard and Catelyn Stark. He was named after his deceased uncle, Brandon.', 'id': 'e3fc0543-52af-40f7-a4b0-5e68e350f543', 'score': 218.03285, 'probability': 0.8984690445729299, 'question': None, 'meta': {'vector_id': '2220', 'name': '331_Bran_Stark.txt'}, 'embedding': None}, 
#{'text': '\n=== Robb Stark ===\nRobb Stark is the oldest child of Eddard and Catelyn Stark, and the heir to Winterfell. He is not a POV character, but features in the POV chapters of his family members in the first three novels in the series.\nIn the HBO television adaptation, he is portrayed by Richard Madden.', 'id': 'af4010af-6257-46f3-9331-8b0c3fb89298', 'score': 179.93167, 'probability': 0.8580657384755829, 'question': None, 'meta': {'vector_id': '1711', 'name': '30_List_of_A_Song_of_Ice_and_Fire_characters.txt'}, 'embedding': None}, 
#...]}

```

Let me know if this helps or I should clarify any of the steps in more detail. '

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b'Hey @Ierezell , 

The camembert model uses a different tokenizer than the original DPR model. Can you please set `infer_tokenizer_classes=True` when loading the model and see if this already solves your problem? 

```
retriever = DensePassageRetriever(
...
    infer_tokenizer_classes=True

)
```

On another note: If you want to use the titles of your docs during training / inference, you will need to rename the field in your documents from `meta["title"] -> meta["name"]`. If you don't want to use them set `embed_title=False` when initializing DPR. 

Hope this helps!'

Title: b'Simplify CI jobs'
Body:
b'Current CI job have following issues -
- Frequent OOM
- Only test Linux build
- Only text Python 3.7 build
- Missing coverage run
- Missing mypy on rest_api module
- PR feedback about code formatting is very slow


I have following suggestions -
1. Use solution similar to [Azure pipeline](https://github.com/marketplace/azure-pipelines) to test build on Linux, MacOS and Windows (Also we need to tag some tests with env as well, like faiss tests may fail on Windows so with tag we can disable them)
2. Use [Tox](https://tox.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) to test build on all python supported versions (3.6, 3.7, 3.8 and 3.9)
3. Use Black or Flake8 along with mypy and pylint, static code checker in separate CI job to get fast code feedback
4. Use coverage to collect code coverage information via pytest (for first we will not block merge, but later merge can me blocked if PR does not have good code coverage)
5. Move slow tests to separate CI jobs to mitigate OOM issue.
6. Enable parallel test run

Please correct or suggest better options as well.'

Title: b'Question on FAQ Retrieval Tutorial -- with FAISS I get different performance'
Body:
b'**Question**
Hi, I went through the [FAQ tutorial](https://haystack.deepset.ai/docs/latest/tutorial4md), and I applied it to a dataset I am working on (it's public and can be downloaded [here](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1KfPgHZ5NXjKPYAZToYExL6e8DHAxPfC8?usp=sharing) for reproducibility of the issue). I want to use FAISS because I will mainly do dense similarity retrieval. However, the implementation with FAISS gives me a much lower performance than the implementation with ElasticSearch. Why is this the case?

My understanding is that the embeddings are computed using the retriever, which doesn't vary according to which document store I pick. Embeddings of query and questions should be the same, and the similarity computation the same. Is that right?


**Additional context**
You can check my example in [this notebook](https://github.com/AMChierici/dm_api/blob/main/dm.ipynb). Please note in this notebook I am using InMeemoryDocumentStore instead of FAISS because I needed to save the index as a pickle file, and the FAISS format didn't allow me to. But if I change the document store to FAISS, the performance is the same.

I replaced this code block from the original tutorial:
```
document_store = ElasticsearchDocumentStore(host="localhost", username="", password="",
                                            index="document",
                                            embedding_field="question_emb",
                                            embedding_dim=768,
                                            excluded_meta_data=["question_emb"])
```

With this one:
```
document_store = InMemoryDocumentStore(similarity="cosine")
```

Then I also had to change `finder.get_answers_via_similar_questions` for retrieving answers because it was returning an empty list. I used `document_store.query_by_embedding` instead (for both the FAISS and the InMemory document stores).

When I compute the no. of hits @1 and @10 (hits within the first one and ten top retrieved answers, respectively), I get 0.4411764705882353
0.6058823529411764
with the InMemory document store (and FAISS too, same numbers).

Instead, I get much better results with the Elastic Search document store. Namely, 0.58 and 0.71.
'

Title: b'tholor'
Body: b'@AMChierici Thanks for reporting. We will have a look. @julian-risch Can you please try to replicate and understand the root cause? Might be related to #672 . '

Title: b'julian-risch'
Body: b'@AMChierici Thank you for providing code and data to replicate this issue. Much appreciated. You are right that we would expect the same performance form the different document stores (FAISS and ElasticSearch) because they use the same document similarity measure. Let me have a look into it.'

Title: b'julian-risch'
Body: b'Hello @AMChierici and first of all sorry for taking so long to get back to you. I think the problem is about different settings for the similarity metric. With elasticsearch you need to use `similarity = "cosine"` and with the other document stores you need to use `similarity = "dot_product"` to have a fair comparison with the same settings. Sorry for the confusion.\r\nPlease try to use `FAISSDocumentStore(similarity="dot_product")` and see whether you get the expected results.'

Title: b'AMChierici'
Body:
b'Thank you, @julian-risch . If I understand correctly, `similarity="dot_product"` is the default in `FAISSDocumentStore` and I can't use `similarity="cosine"` in `FAISSDocumentStore`.

I realized the error was another one. When I used the doc store, it connected automatically to another MySQL DB that was already available with some repeated questions and answers. Therefore the metric was giving me different outcomes.

Could you please clarify if my understanding of the first paragraphs was correct?'

Title: b'julian-risch'
Body: b'Your understanding of the FAISSDocumentStore is correct: `similarity="dot_product"` is the default and other similarity metrics are currently not supported.\r\nHappy to hear that you were able to resolve the issue @AMChierici . Thanks for letting us know. I will close this issue then.'

Title: b'Annotation tool: unanswerable questions'
Body:
b"**Question**
Hi, 
I am wondering, if it's possible to create unanswerable questions with the annotation tool like the ones in SQuAD 2.0.

**Additional context**
In SQuAD 2.0 the crowd workers were asked to create unanswerable questions in addition to answerable ones. 
I couldn't find the option to do so with the annotation tool. In your opinion, does it make sense to have unanswerable questions in the training data?
"

Title: b'Timoeller'
Body:
b'hey @sophgit thanks for using the annotation tool.

You are right, we do not have the option to contruct squad 2.0 style unanserable questions. Only if you have predefined questions you can choose the option "answer not given".
For predefined question chosse the annotation mode "Answer category". Then there is an import option for questions via CSVs.

Currently we do not actively develop the annottation tool much, so getting the feature of unanswerable question inside might take some time, depending on the usefulness. What use case do you have in mind and did you already experiment with no_answer questions and their value for you case?'

Title: b'sophgit'
Body:
b'Thanks @Timoeller for your fast reply. :)
Currently I am only using the custom questions, thus I didn't know about the no_answer feature for predefined questions.
My QA system is supposed to work for CRM data and company/product specific data.
I have not yet worked with no_answer questions. I just thought, in order for people to trust my QA system it would be better, if the system replies with "no answer found" than with an incorrect answer. And therefore my approach would have been to create  training data with some more unanswerable questions. But I can try using the predefined questions to do so.'

Title: b'tholor'
Body: b'You could also try a short-term hack: \r\nAdd a "special token" at the start of every of your doc that you upload (.e.g "<No Answer>"). If annotators don\'t find an answer they mark this token. Later you can easily convert those labels to proper "no answers" in the exported SQuAD file.'

Title: b'sophgit'
Body: b"that's a cool idea, thanks @tholor!"

Title: b'Timoeller'
Body: b'Nice @tholor, that would be an option to create unanswerable questions. I would propose to create a special token at the end of the text, so you can remove it afterwards and not mess up answer offsets.\r\n\r\nAm I right that for your CRM data you already have predefined questions? If so, uploading them to the tool and marking them as unanswerable would be the easiest. Though be aware that especially for long text it is extremely timeconsuming to label unanswerable questions. People have to go through the whole text before being able to say the answer is really not present.'

Title: b'Timoeller'
Body:
b'Hey @SasikiranJ that is indeed a good question (I reformulated the issue title accordingly). The ability of Question Answering Models to generalize to out of domain data (your custom documents) is an ongoing research topic.
For an up to date reference please have a look at the [EMNLP 20202 paper](https://www.aclweb.org/anthology/2020.emnlp-main.190/)

To give you some condensed guidance:
- In general Language Models used for Question Answering are very powerful and intelligent. They "understand" the question and context documents. To give a few examples of the capabilities: The model has knowledge about similar terms (understands synonyms) and words in context (the apple that falls from the tree is different to the apple that needs a software update) and relates questions starting with "who" to answers that contain a name of a person. 
- Sometimes the model just memorizes training examples and applies the connection of question and answer to "unseen" test examples.
- Out of domain questions and texts can be very similar to the data the model was trained on - so it only seems the model can generalize.


How good the model generalizes to your custom documents, you best annotate a couple of question answer pairs and see how the model performs. '

Title: b'Updating Embeddings for Faiss DPR on Large Dataset (Batchmode)'
Body:
b"**Question**
As mentioned in the title, I'm trying to update the embeddings for Faiss (HNSW) with a DPR retriever on a large dataset (~15 million documents). Following the tutorial steps, I'm writing the documents to a local sqlite db (~15 gb .db). However, calling update_embeddings uses all my RAM (64 GB) and all my swap (64 GB) and proceeds to run out of memory after running for hours. I'm fairly certain the line that's consuming so much memory is: https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/3f81c93f36519ab78213f145c699ce7df2c4ddf8/haystack/document_store/faiss.py#L158

More specifically: https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/3f81c93f36519ab78213f145c699ce7df2c4ddf8/haystack/document_store/sql.py#L124
The call to query.all() is what's causing the issue.

I'm not very familiar with SQLAlchemy and SQLite in general but it seems that there is some inefficient usage of space when querying the DB. Is there an alternative way with dealing with large datasets like this? It would be preferable if there was a batch option to update_embeddings so that a group of embeddings would be flushed to disk before proceeding.

On a side note, some type of progress indicator or option to enable one when calling write_documents or update_embeddings would be useful (considering these operations can take an hour or more)."

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b'Hey @vinchg , 

Thanks for raising this issue. It's highly relevant. 

So in general: for larger datasets like this, we would recommend not using SQLite but rather Postgres. 
You can easily spin one up via a Docker: 
``` 
docker run --name haystack-postgres -p 5432:5432 -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=password -d postgres
docker exec -it haystack-postgres psql -U postgres -c "CREATE DATABASE haystack;"
``` 

and then connect in Python via: 
```
document_store = FAISSDocumentStore(sql_url="postgresql://postgres:password@localhost:5432/haystack",
                                            faiss_index_factory_str=index_type)
```

However, this will probably only increase memory efficiency but not resolve the underlying problem. 
I totally agree that we should add some batch functionality to `update_embeddings` and a tqdm progress bar.

> The call to query.all() is what's causing the issue.

Do you have already any embeddings in the document store or is that a fresh one?

> Is there an alternative way with dealing with large datasets like this?

As a temporary workaround, you could generate the embeddings in batches yourself before calling `write_documents()` and attach them to your documents before writing to the DocumentStore. Rough sketch: 

```
from haystack import Document
dicts = [{"text": "some text"}, ...]
docs = [Document.from_dict(d) for d in dicts]

# get the embedding for a batch of docs
batch_docs = docs[:32]
batch_emb = retriever.embed_passages(batch_docs)

# attach embeddings to the docs
for emb, doc in zip(batch_emb, batch_docs):
    doc.embedding = emb
...

# later: write everything to the doc store
doc_store.write_documents(all_docs)
```

Again, we should in any case add the batch functionality soon in `update_embeddings()` to simplify usage here ...

@lalitpagaria Would this maybe be something that is of interest to you and you would like to work on? If not, @tanaysoni can take care of it.  
'

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b'Hey @BasicLich , 

It depends a bit on the content of your markdown. If you have a lot of formatting syntax in there (e.g. many headlines, bold, italics ...) stripping this out will results in slightly better speed (fewer tokens for the model) and probably slightly better quality (tokens like \*\*some\*\* could be tokenized better with some models).

If you decide for implementing a stripping step, I would suggest implementing a `MarkdownConverter` class that inherits from our [BaseConverter](https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/master/haystack/file_converter/base.py). While it could only do basic stripping in the beginning, I see more useful functionalities down the road (e.g. parsing titles of sections as "meta data" => very useful for retrieval with DPR). Would be great to see a PR for this and we are happy to support you along the way / add some extra functionality ...

'

But need to add extra dependency of  `BeautifulSoup`.\r\n- Using `Tika`: Convert markdown to html and then pass that to `tika` which support html extraction.'

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b'Hey @gabinguo, 

Thanks for reporting this. It is a known limitation (see https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/issues/601) and we will introduce a batch mode for `update_embeddings` soon. As a temporary workaround (that we also use internally) you can create the embeddings first in batches, attach them to the document and then call write_documents(). See a rough sketch here: https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/issues/601#issuecomment-729469535
Let me know if you have further questions on this workaround. Otherwise, I will keep you updated and ping you here once we implemented the batch_mode ... '

Title: b'Ram Issue in Tutorial 9 (DPR Training) Colab'
Body:
b'When running the DPR Training tutorial in Colab, the download of the training dataset seems to run fine, but the program crashes before starting to download the dev file due to running out of RAM.
```python
# Download original DPR data
# WARNING: the train set is 7.4GB and the dev set is 800MB

s3_url_train = "https://dl.fbaipublicfiles.com/dpr/data/retriever/biencoder-nq-train.json.gz"

fetch_archive_from_http(s3_url_train, output_dir=doc_dir + "train/")
fetch_archive_from_http(s3_url_dev, output_dir=doc_dir + "dev/")
```
We need to find some way to reduce this RAM consumption. It likely has something to do with the way the files are being uncompressed
```python
def fetch_archive_from_http(url: str, output_dir: str, proxies: Optional[dict] = None):
            ...
            elif url[-3:] == ".gz":
                json_bytes = gzip.open(temp_file.name).read()
                filename = url.split("/")[-1].replace(".gz", "")
                output_filename = Path(output_dir) / filename
                output = open(output_filename, "wb")
                output.write(json_bytes)
            else:

```'

Title: b'lalitpagaria'
Body:
b'Actually following line read whole file in memory also decompress it in memory as well. 
```
json_bytes = gzip.open(temp_file.name).read()
```
Python 3 support buffered reading automatically so if change it to as follows memory utilization will improve -
```
            elif url[-3:] == ".gz":
                filename = url.split("/")[-1].replace(".gz", "")
                output_filename = Path(output_dir) / filename
                with gzip.open(temp_file.name) as f, open(output_filename, "wb") as output:
                        for line in f:
                               output.write(line)
```
I have not tested above snippet, I will do tonight. If this not work fine there is another solution to read file in [chunks](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/34632521/downloading-a-large-file-in-chunks-with-gzip-encoding-python-3-4). But I don't think the would be necessary as gzip already support buffered IO.

One more point we can directly uncompress file from url instead of download to temp file and uncompressing it. Python compression libs have streaming support. Refer this https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/issues/709#issuecomment-755654431'

The method _certifi.where()_ returns the reference to the installed certificate authority (CA) bundle.  (https://pypi.org/project/certifi/)

Title: b'antoniolanza1996'
Body:
b"Here https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/e9b5439b00690a92b9e385cae341d47a803f20d5/haystack/document_store/elasticsearch.py#L92
Haystack feeds `ca_certs` to this Elasticsearch Python Client and, as you can see [here](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch-py/blob/383d6a401a4a015e9cefc84a50063524baf4266b/elasticsearch/client/__init__.py#L113-L121), this parameter is not handled as a boolean. Instead, you have to feed a path to the CA cert.

Indeed, using `ca_certs=certifi.where()` and a Google Colab VM, I have been able to connect an `ElasticsearchDocumentStore` with an Elasticsearch instance from https://www.elastic.co with SSL support.

Title: b'julian-risch'
Body: b'Thank you for reporting this problem. I was able to reproduce it. It seems that it is caused by the squad processors multiprocessing code. It is specific to running the code on Windows. If I am not mistaken, right now the multiprocessing imports the calling module (your tutorial code) and tries to execute it for every subprocess. As you reported, consequently it tries to start elasticsearch multiple times and as a result, there are error messages "permission denied" and "failed to obtain node locks". Let me see how to fix this...'

Title: b'julian-risch'
Body:
b'You need to encapsulate your code/the tutorial code in a function, e.g., `your_code()`. Then you can call this function from within a guard that ensures the code is executed only once and not by every spawned subprocess during the multiprocessing:

```
def yourcode():
    # In Colab / No Docker environments: Start Elasticsearch from source
    es_server = Popen([os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__),
                                'elasticsearch-7.10.1/bin/elasticsearch.bat')], shell=True)
...
...
    print_answers(prediction, details="minimal")
```
```
if __name__ == '__main__':
    your_code()
```
@Rob192 @Victor7095 Please let me know, if it works for you with this small change. Thank you.'

Title: b'brandenchan'
Body:
b'Hey @antoniolanza1996 so we dug deeper and actually found that there quite a few differences between FARM and transformer Readers that would contribute to this kind of divergence. Bottom line is that we think both Readers are currently working as they are designed, albeit differently from each other.

What I suspect causes the biggest difference between the two models are the following two points:

- In Transformers, start and end logits are normalized with softmax in each passage (https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/ccbf74a685ae24bd1a0ba1325e4e9a9d62bbb2fa/src/transformers/pipelines.py#L1357). This makes comparisons between answers found in different parts of the text less effective. FARM does not apply the softmax thus making logits more comparable.

- In HuggingFace, start and end logits are multiplied (https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/ccbf74a685ae24bd1a0ba1325e4e9a9d62bbb2fa/src/transformers/pipelines.py#L1415) while in FARM they are added (https://github.com/deepset-ai/FARM/blob/99c2694587e6a573012d1fa7c2b8d7eca8a888ab/farm/modeling/prediction_head.py#L1072). We suspect that this results in Transformers returning a greater diversity of answers while FARM is more primed to return overlapping spans as answers. 

There are also some more minor differences:

- For one, the tokenization using Roberta models is slightly different. In practice this should not make a substatial difference but it has to do with how the Roberta tokenizer treats words that have a whitespace before them and words that don't. If you're interested in understanding this more, check out this issue(https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues/1196), this part of the FARM code (https://github.com/deepset-ai/FARM/blob/99c2694587e6a573012d1fa7c2b8d7eca8a888ab/farm/modeling/tokenization.py#L297) and contrast how the Transformers pipeline calls the tokenizer.

- We've seen also that in the Transformers reader, the model can predict the exact same answer twice with two different scores if it occurs in a section of text that is in two "sliding windows". This has to do with how documents are split into smaller passages that can be passed into the model. In FARM, we remove such duplicates.

Not sure what level of familiarity you have with QA systems but if you want a primer on sliding windows, logit calculations and aggreation, I'd point you to this! (https://medium.com/deepset-ai/modern-question-answering-systems-explained-4d0913744097)

I hope this helps and if you'd like me to clarify anything that I mentioned above, just let me know. I'd be more than happy to try and explain.

'

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b'Hey @mchari, 

If you use batch size one, your batch will contain 1x query, 1x positive passage and 1x hard negative passage.
It's highly recommended to increase the batch size as you will only then benefit from the "in-batch negatives" and create enough training signal for convergence. The original DPR authors recommend 16 (https://github.com/facebookresearch/DPR#best-hyperparameter-settings).

Title: b'tanaysoni'
Body:
b'Hi @gabinguo, I see two potential issues with the custom_query
  
- the field for the name in the custom query should be `name` instead of `meta.name`. In Elasticsearch, all fields are flattened, so there's no higher level `meta` key present 
- the name field should be set to type `text` if you want to do a query. With `keyword`, Elasticsearch would look for an exact match 

Let me know if the issue is resolved with these changes.


---- 

>  elasticsearch query to retrieve in a big document collection

You could try out splitting large documents using the [Preprocessing module](https://haystack.deepset.ai/docs/latest/preprocessingmd#Preprocessing). This will enable more granular document retrieval with Elasticsearch and also optimize the `Reader` speed as it'll have to scan smaller documents. You can find recommendations for document length [here](https://haystack.deepset.ai/docs/latest/optimizationmd#Document-Length).

>  I thought the title could help a bit

You could experiement with per field boosting option for the `multi_match` query. For instance, if you want to add a 2x boost for the title, you can set the `multi_match` fields to `"fields" : [ "title^2", "text" ]`.
'

This seems very slow. What GPU / AWS instance type are you using (RAM is not so important for inference speed)?

I could still see some potential in reducing the split length. If I got you right, you currently feed 5 docs with ~ 50k chars each to the reader. With our new `Preprocessor` class, you can also split based on the number of words while respecting sentence boundaries. I would really try to reduce this as much as possible until you see a drop in answer accuracy. 

In a CPU environment, using the onnx-runtime can yield significant speed-ups. We have this already available in FARM (https://github.com/deepset-ai/FARM/blob/master/farm/modeling/adaptive_model.py#L541). However, it's not integrated yet upstream in Haystack's `FARMReader`. Another thing you could explore if you are not already using it: multiprocessing for the preprocessing. You can specify the number of processes via `FARMReader(num_processes=...)`

Regarding, the models, I would also encourage you to try MiniLM again with the latest FARM version (0.5.0). We got a 5x speed improvement on a certain type of questions (where it's hard to find the answer or there's no answer) due to some better vectorization in the postprocessing.

Title: b'Updating Embeddings for Faiss DPR on Big Dataset very slow'
Body:
b'It seems to me that updating embedding for Faiss DPR on big dataset is quite slow. 
I'm fairly certain the problem is in this call of function _get_predictions in DPR:
dataset, tensor_names, baskets = self.processor.dataset_from_dicts(
            dicts, indices=[i for i in range(len(dicts))], return_baskets=True
        )

It tries to convert documents to datasets. When the number of documents is around 100,000, this call takes about half hour. But if the number of documents is around 400,000, this call takes almost forever.

It seems we are using a single worker to process the documents. We can improve by parallel processing and batch processing.

Another thing I notice is that we store all embedding in GPU when we do the prediction for passages. I'm not sure it will work if we have a big dataset:
all_embeddings = {"query": torch.tensor([]).to(self.device), "passages": torch.tensor([]).to(self.device)}

In the end, I want to thank you guys for such a wonderful package. In just 2 days, I built a question and answering demo with your great tool. You guys are awesome!

Thanks,

Nick'

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b"Hey Nick,

Thanks for reporting! 

We will investigate it: 

**1. Speed of `processor.dataset_from_dicts`**
We should first check if there's potential to optimize the processing function directly. 
Do you use the fast tokenizers for DPR via `use_fast_tokenizers=True` in the DPR init?
Similar to other parts of Haystack (DPR Training, Reader inference ...), we could of course leverage multiprocessing here. We just wanted to keep it as simple as possible here and didn't see this bottleneck in preprocessing with the fast Tokenizers yet.
But if multiprocessing speeds it up significantly, we should add it here ...

**2. Memory efficiency of  `all_embeddings`**
We will introduce a batch mode for `update_embeddings`. This should resolve your concern and we don't need to bother about `all_embeddings` in the lower level `_get_predictions()`. See #601. 
"

Title: b'Refactor "most similar search" to be more generic'
Body:
b'**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
As of now we have two main usage scenarios in haystack: 
- Extractive QA (retriever + reader)
- "FAQ based QA" (only retriever; find most similar question)

- "Semantic document search" (Retriever only; very similar to FAQ case but more generic documents)

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b"Hi @x0rzkov,

It's definitely possible to integrate it as Haystack is highly modular. You would need to create a `ManticoreDocumentStore` class that implements the main methods from `BaseDocumentStore` for indexing and querying (see [here](https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/c0c2865e58b09570d525e5a778cf0b39e7cc25b9/haystack/database/base.py#L189)). For a basic version, you'll probably be fine with skipping the label/eval methods there and just focus on the essential ones like `write_documents()`, `get_document_by_id`, `get_all_documents`.

As Manticore has still a fairly small user group, the integration is not on our immediate roadmap. However, we would be open to a PR if you are interested in working on this and we can support you along the way.   

 "

Title: b'Refactor Finder to allow more flexibility (multiple retrievers, pure document search ...)'
Body:
b"**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**

The finder was initially designed to wrap a **single retriever** and a **single reader** to do **extractive** QA.
As Haystack is growing and covering more use cases we need to rethink the design to allow: 
- multiple retrievers (see #125)
- a generator instead of a reader to do generative QA
- pure document search (retriever only, see #420)
- reader only 
- more complex routing patterns in the future (e.g. classify if a request is a question, if yes => reader, if no => pure retriever)
- optional: Having multiple retrievers in series instead of parallel. Inspired by passage reranking methods. See [this blog's section on two stage ranking](https://searchengineland.com/could-google-passage-indexing-be-leveraging-bert-342975)

**To consider:**
- Should be easy to exchange reader with generator (e.g. same API endpoint?)
- Midterm: Import/Export config that describes whole setup

**Some thoughts to get started...**

=> Single vs. Multiple Finder classes? 

**Option B) Single Finder**
get_answers()
- faq, generative, extractive
- can we optimize the return format to cover all cases nicely?
get_documents()

**Option A) Multiple Finders**
a) splitting into faq, generative, extractive
b) DocFinder QAFinder => we don't gain much except clearer init
2) One vs. splitting get_answers()? generate_answer, faq_answer ...
3) Passing List of retrievers vs. Finder.add(retriever) + Finder.add(retriever) + Finder.add(reader)
4) Redesign API endpoints (e.g. `doc-qa` still right naming?)

I'd lean towards...
=> Single Finder
=> get_answers() get_documents()
=> API: documents object (ids+meta)
=> remove get_answers_via_similar...()

Open question: FAQ via get_documents() or via get_answers()"

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b'Quick Update: 

We are currently thinking bigger here. With Haystack, we already have many nice "lego building blocks". However, we are missing a flexible, powerful way of sticking them together. Instead of having rather rigid `Finder` classes, we, therefore, think of introducing a highly flexible `Pipeline` class that is using a Directed Acyclic Graph under the hood (a bit like Apache Airflow). 

You could add "tasks" as nodes (Retriever, Reader, Generator ...) and route your query via edges. This could cover not only all of the above use cases, but would also allow many other, more complex search pipelines that we have in mind for the future. 

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1563902/98772615-6a229180-23e7-11eb-87da-2ecddede5e84.png)

Happy to hear your feedback on this direction!
 

'

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b"As of now, we support the following workflow for FAQ-style QA (get_answers_via_similar_questions):

- Collect feedback via API endpoint `/faq-qa-feedback`
- Export the collected feedback via API endpoint `/export-faq-qa-feedback`
- Use the data to train/fine-tune a model **externally** (e.g. using sentence-transformers)
- Load this model back in Haystack

While training of extractive QA models on collected feedback is already supported **internally** in Haystack, we don't have this functionality for FAQ-QA on our roadmap right now. Of course, we are open for contributions from the community here."

Title: b'brandenchan'
Body:
b"Hi @mathieudumayet, that's a great question! The QA models that Haystack uses are not explicitly trained to resolve this ambiguity. But often you can deduce how the model interpreted the pronoun based on the answer it gives back.

While I'm not an expert in this field, I think what you're really asking about is the task of coreference resolution, for which there is quite some literature. Here's a [link](https://demo.allennlp.org/coreference-resolution) to a demo coreference resolution system.

Not quite the same but still related is the [Winograd schema challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winograd_Schema_Challenge#Origin) which asks models to perform a kind of coreference resolution on ambiguous pronouns. This generally tests the ability of the model to apply some kind of world knowledge to get to the right answer.

Does this help?"

Body: b'Hey @tholor , quick question. If I wish to extend the vocabulary of a model, will it suffice if I directly add new words of a domain specific corpus in the existing vocab file? Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b"> will it suffice if I directly add new words of a domain specific corpus in the existing vocab file?

Short answer: No, unfortunately not. The model won't have any embeddings trained for these tokens.
Long answer: In some models (e.g. bert-base) there are some placeholders in the vocab file (e.g. [Unused001]). You can replace those with domain specific tokens, but then you would still need to continue masked language model training. In your case, I would not do that as training the multilingual model on a turkish corpus will let it forget about other languages and then you could better directly take a turkish model (e.g. https://github.com/stefan-it/turkish-bert) 
 
> If I take the vocab of a multilingual model and instead of doing masked language modelling add the new words, will that work?

No, without training the model has no understanding about the new words in the vocab

As I believe there's currently no Turkish QA dataset, the best thing you can do is probably taking a multilingual model (e.g. XLM-R)  which was trained on multilingual or english QA datasets (see my comment above) and potentially create a small turkish QA dataset for your domain where you can continue fine-tuning. 
As an alternative for a dedicated labeling process (which can be time consuming), you could also consider to collect feedback from the users of your QA system (via :+1: / :-1: ). We have an [API endpoint](https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/master/rest_api/controller/feedback.py#L66) to collect this feedback, store it in the DocumentStore and export it in SQuAD format for model training. It's currently not very well documented, but we will add some more infos soon."

Title: b'brandenchan'
Body:
b'Hi, so from a quick glance, it seems there is already a [Thai BERT](https://github.com/google-research/bert/issues/204) out there  and they report that it performs better than multilingual BERT. 

Its worth noting that if you want to do QA with this model, you will need a Thai extractive Question Answering dataset as well i.e. something similar to SQuAD. There are two multilingual QA datasets which actually include Thai: [XQuAD](https://github.com/deepmind/xquad) and [Tydi](https://github.com/google-research-datasets/tydiqa). XQuAD is generally only used as an evaluation dataset and Id expect there to be only about 1k examples for Thai. Thats not enough to train the QA model. However, Tydi should contain about 20k Thai examples which should produce a decent result! [This article I wrote about non-English QA](https://medium.com/deepset-ai/going-beyond-squad-part-1-question-answering-in-different-languages-8eac6cf56f21) might be of interest to you, especially the section about multilingual QA.

As mentioned above, the quickest way to get a baseline QA model running is to use a multilingual language model that has been trained to QA datasets in other languages. To explain, deepset/xlm-robert-large-squad2 is a multilingual language model trained on English Squad2. Through zero-shot learning, the model has learned a little bit about question answering regardless of language. In theory it should be able to do a little bit of Thai QA. Weve found that its performance isnt very strong, but it is definitely a useful baseline. This model can always be retrained with language specific data in order to improve!'

Title: b'How to process documents in different (for example Russian) language (need a tutorial)'
Body: b'How to use documents in different (for example Russian) language (need a tutorial)\r\nWhat will be the settings for Retreiver and Reader?\r\n'

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b'Hi @aleh4d ,

This depends a bit on the language that we are talking. Depending on the language there are different types of retrievers / readers available. 

Let me try to give you an overview of the options **for Russian** (and many of that will hold for other languages): 

## Retriever
**1) Recommended: ElasticsearchRetriever**
Solid baseline and can be adjusted quite easily to any language. See Elasticsearch's documentation for the[ available language-specific analyzers](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/analysis-lang-analyzer.html) and [how to switch them](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/specify-analyzer.html)  

**2) Dense (EmbeddingRetriever / DPR):** 
These are more powerful than Elasticsearch, but AFAIK unfortunately not available for Russian yet. However, as these methods currently gain quite some popularity, I am pretty sure that we will see models being published for other languages soon.

## Reader
You can find some thoughts on that in our [documentation](https://haystack.deepset.ai/docs/latest/readermd#Languages-other-than-English), but happy to go into a few more details here.

**1) Recommended: Monolingual Russian model**
There is a Russian QA dataset called [SberQUAD](https://www.groundai.com/project/sberquad-russian-reading-comprehension-dataset-description-and-analysis/1). From a quick look, I couldn't find a model on Huggingface's model hub yet. So I'd recommend: Download the dataset from [here](http://files.deeppavlov.ai/datasets/sber_squad-v1.1.tar.gz) and train your own model. Simply adjust this [Haystack tutorial](https://colab.research.google.com/github/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/master/tutorials/Tutorial2_Finetune_a_model_on_your_data.ipynb) and run: 
``` 
from haystack.reader.farm import FARMReader
# Use "rubert" - a Russian BERT model
reader = FARMReader(model_name_or_path="DeepPavlov/rubert-base-cased", use_gpu=True)
# Your downloaded sberquad folder from above:
train_data = "data/sber_squad"
reader.train(data_dir=train_data, train_filename="train-v1.1.json", dev_filename="dev-v1.1.json",use_gpu=True, batch_size=16 n_epochs=2, save_dir="rubert-base-cased-sberquad")
``` 
If you need further help with this let us know! We're happy to support with brain or GPU resources.  I am sure there are more in the community that would benefit from this!
 
**2) Alternative: Multilingual model**
There's always the option of using a multilingual model. Usually, the performance is worse than with a monolingual one. Example models: 
- deepset/xlm-roberta-large-squad2 
- mrm8488/bert-multi-cased-finedtuned-xquad-tydiqa-goldp 
- mrm8488/bert-multi-cased-finetuned-xquadv1 
- mrm8488/bert-multi-uncased-finetuned-xquadv1 
- mrm8488/distilbert-multi-finetuned-for-xqua-on-tydiqa 
- mrm8488/xlm-multi-finetuned-xquadv1 
(see [here](https://huggingface.co/models?filter=question-answering,multilingual))

Hope this helps!

@brandenchan I think this could be a good topic for a more detailed "guide" in our documentation. We already have a section for readers, but it could be nice to have one central piece where everything is combined (retriever, reader ...). 

'

Title: b'Sliding window for Dense Passage Retriever'
Body:
b"**Question**
Hello good people from haystack,

I am currently experimenting with the Dense Passage Retriever and I wanted to ask a quick question
Assuming I am working with longer documents (>1000 characters) and I use a reader with sliding window, for instance:
`reader = FARMReader(... max_seq_len=512, doc_stride=50 ...)`

Wouldn't it make sense to also use a sliding window when embedding the documents for the retrieval stage with the Dense Passage Retriever. I see that I can set the `max_seq_len`, but no sliding window?
Is there a reason why the underlying BERT model does not allow for a sliding window?


"

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b'Hey @jonas-nothnagel ,

You are right that DPR cuts texts at `max_seq_len` and only those first tokens will be considered for creating the embedding. 
The current best practice is to do the splitting of docs at preprocessing time, i.e. 
1) split your docs into smaller chunks (e.g. hard cut at "100 words" like in the original DPR paper) 
2) add them to the documentstore via `document_store.write_documents()`

Doing this at preprocessing time rather than in the retriever itself via a sliding window has a few advantages, incl.: 
- 1-to-1 mapping between docs and embeddings in the documentstore (with a sliding window you would probably have N embeddings per doc)
- passing shorter docs from the retriever to the reader which accelerates inference significantly
- no computational overhead at inference time

We are already working on a simpler usage of preprocessing in Haystack (#378) and want to include some further options for splitting (e.g. word-based splits, respecting sentence boundaries ...). 

 

'

Title: b'nsankar'
Body:
b'@jonas-nothnagel  
@tholor  This is an interesting and perhaps a fairly complex data preprocessing problem to solve in order to get meaningful answers instead of partial answers. (i.e respecting sentence boundaries in the text content while using the max_sequence_length). This is one of the areas I am stuck with DPR in terms of the relevance of answers and exploring preprocessing options. I am exploring senetence detection with custom boundries using spacy as cited in an example in this web site.. ( https://realpython.com/natural-language-processing-spacy-python/ )

It would be good to try when task #378 is made available.

'

Title: b'jonas-nothnagel'
Body:
b'In general, it feels like data preprocessing is really the key for a successful QA system (and probably almost all ML tasks). 

@nsankar Assuming we use something like spacy and chunk the text into sentences (further assuming our text comes in a well-processable format with proper punctuations and sentences), would you consider re-merging sentences back to longer paragraphs (<512 tokens of course) before feeding into the DPR? I do not have a computational base for this argument, but I feel like there must be threshold, where providing too many candidates for a retriever will also significantly worsen the performance. 

Perhaps it would be interesting to find a way to also base the pre-processing on the kind of questions we want to ask. If we are sure that the answers to our questions are single tokens, contained in clearly distinguishable sentences, then splitting on sentence level may be useful, however, if the answers to the questions are mostly longer phrases or whole sentences then we probably should not chunk down to individual sentences. 

Excited to see outcomes of https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/issues/378 '

Title: b'nsankar'
Body: b'@jonas-nothnagel     As to your question about longer paragraphs,   this is exactly what I have been thinking about. Either we should be able to extract the paragraphs within the token length of 512 or smaller or assemble the sentences in to paras.   Once there is a way to prepare text in this manner, I believe it requires some extensive testing and observations with different types of content / size.\r\n\r\nAlso as you said, the type of question /answer can matter. For instance the sort of answers relevant for a factoid and non-factoid scenario.'

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b'>  I do not have a computational base for this argument, but I feel like there must be threshold, where providing too many candidates for a retriever will also significantly worsen the performance.

I have a similar gut feeling, that single sentences would be problematic for many retrievers. Even in cases where the answer is just contained in a single sentence, the bigger "topic" / "context" is only clear from a few sentences. 

>Once there is a way to prepare text in this manner, I believe it requires some extensive testing and observations with different types of content / size.

Yep, I think there won't be a single perfect splitting + cleaning config for all datasets and languages. However, some experiments here could help to understand a bit better in what scenarios, which preprocessing option is preferable.

We are currently implementing a few options in #473  '

Title: b'tholor'
Body: b'A basic version was implemented in #473 that, for example, allows splitting longer texts every 100 words with a sliding window and respecting sentence boundaries (do not split in the middle of a sentence). \r\n'

Title: b'Timoeller'
Body:
b'I am not aware of any papers or blog posts about better QA model confidence and correct handling of no_answer. Unfortunately the no_answer handling is rather complex - though I am sure you could dig into it with a bit of our help : )

**Some Background**
In the official squad eval script there is the option to include "na_prob_file" scores and do some analysis on it. But getting this na_prob_file is currently not possible in FARM nor haystack.

**Explanation of no_ans_boost**
The no_ans_boost is changing the no_answer_logit, so positive values make predicting no_ans more likely. Hence the naming "boost". You could try out different boost values to see how your predictions change. But this is a lot of tedious and manual work. 

In the end what you need is the no_answer score compared to the text answer score, aggregated over all predictions. This value called "max_no_ans_gap" is returned in the results dictionary (when doing FARMReader.predict()) and computed in this function: https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/55552741702dd18384d9b38a436d9c96fb2fdf10/haystack/reader/base.py#L22
You could collect the max_no_ans_gap value for all your QA pairs and see how much you would need to change no_ans_boost in order to optimally return the no_answer.'

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b'Hey @alpaltnsy , 

The DPR signature has changed from 0.4.0 -> 0.5.0: 
``` 
# old
DensePassageRetriever(
                  ...
                 max_seq_len: int = 256,
                 ...
                 )

# new 
 DensePassageRetriever(
                  ...
                 max_seq_len_query: int = 64,
                 max_seq_len_passage: int = 256,
                  ...
                 ):
``` 
We decided to split `max_seq_len` into two params, as you usually want to pick way smaller values for the query. 
See also the "breaking changes" in the [release notes](https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/releases/tag/v0.5.0) for more details.'

Title: b'Fix retriever evaluation metrics'
Body:
b'In retriever evaluation you compute `"mean avg precision"` but this is correct only when `open_domain=False`. When `open_domain=True`, this measure isn't MAP but it is MRR because you're considering only the first correct hit.

Useful reference:
- https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/127041/mean-average-precision-vs-mean-reciprocal-rank (see answer, it's very well explained)
- https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/pdf/08eval.pdf (page 9-10)
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evaluation_measures_(information_retrieval)#Mean_average_precision
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_reciprocal_rank

I see two possible scenarios:
1. just change its name in MRR;
2. implement also real MAP for open-domaincontext.

However, in both these scenarios, the return values will differ based on whether you use `open_domain=True` or `open_domain=False`.'

Title: b'antoniolanza1996'
Body:
b"Hi @bogdankostic ,
when I have opened this issue I thought that:
- `open_domain=True` ---> you can have multiple documents which can answer your question;
- `open_domain=False` ---> only one document ID can answer your question (like SQuAD (i.e. reading comprehension task)).

For this reason, I've suggested that MAP is ok for `open_domain=False` because when you have only one possible relevant document, MAP == MRR.

However, as I can see from your first code in https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/pull/547/files#diff-e89fbf9a7a9f7bb1d08741f97417d212c11c9a52cb1f1fc5378097da7d6f07cfR61-R62 , you want to compute MAP and MRR for `open_domain=False` and only MAP for `open_domain=True`. Why?
**IF what I've written at the beginning of this comment for `open_domain` parameter is correct**, I think with your implementation you'll have:
- `open_domain=True` ---> only MAP available... but MRR could also be useful here;
- `open_domain=False` ---> both MAP and MRR, but MAP == MRR.

Instead, **IF what I've written at the beginning of this comment for `open_domain` parameter is NOT correct**, can you please explain me the real behaviour of `open_domain` parameter?"

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b'Hey @antoniolanza1996, 

> open_domain=True ---> you can have multiple documents which can answer your question;
open_domain=False ---> only one document ID can answer your question (like SQuAD (i.e. reading comprehension task)).

Not exactly. We rather refer to "open domain" here as it is used in some recent open domain QA datasets where you just specify a answer string instead of the exact position (e.g. to allow generative QA):  

`open_domain = False` -> Gold documents are **known by IDs** (e.g. in SQuAD),  but there could still be multiple gold docs
`open_domain = True` -> All docs that **include the answer string** are considered as gold documents (similar to [Open NQ](https://github.com/efficientqa/nq-open) or the NQ variant used in the DPR paper).

So from my perspective MRR != MAP for open_domain=False, and we wanted to have one metric that you could compare between both variants. 

> ...  only MAP for open_domain=True

MRR would require us to scan the whole document base for every query to identify the "gold docs". This can get very slow for datasets with millions of docs. We might still add it in the future but it didn't seem worth the effort at this point in time. 

Does this make sense to you?

'

Title: b'antoniolanza1996'
Body:
b'> So from my perspective MRR != MAP for open_domain=False, and we wanted to have one metric that you could compare between both variants.

Yes, with your `open_domain` definition, I agree with you on that. It's worth add both MRR and MAP for `open_domain=False`.

> MRR would require us to scan the whole document base for every query to identify the "gold docs".

Why? MRR considers only the first relevant doc in the `top_k_retriever` documents. You should check only in the first `top_k_retriever` documents and verify if there is one gold document there.


'

Title: b'tholor'
Body: b'Oh yes, sorry. The other way around of course: We only implemented **MRR** for `open_domain=True` - not MAP. '

Title: b'antoniolanza1996'
Body:
b'> We only implemented MRR for open_domain=True - not MAP.

Yes, I see this from @bogdankostic PR. But at this point I think you can compute both measures also for `open_domain=True`. Because MAP consider only the retrieved **AND** relevant documents. Thus, you should check only in the `top_k_retriever` documents and compute average precision. 

The problem you describe (i.e. check in all document base) I think it will come up if you wanna compute _recall_ in standard IR system because for the recall you have to know ALL relevant documents in document base.'

Title: b'tholor'
Body: b"You are right. The **retrieved** docs should actually be enough for precision. I don't know what bug was in my head when I wrote the earlier comment :D"

Title: b'Configuration of DensePassageRetreiver'
Body:
b'**Question**
Hi,
I am new to all of this, so I have a question regarding **max_seq_len** parameter of DPR.

As default, it is set to 256. What does it actually mean? Is it the number of tokens question+passage combined?
If not, what is it? 

I divided my documents into passages which consist of less than 512 tokens each. So I wonder if I would set max_len_seq to be 256 and a passage is larger than 256 token, would DPR ignore half of each passage?

This issue is very crucial to me! :)

Thanks in advance!
**Additional context**
Add any other context or screenshots about the question (optional).
'

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b"Hey @mathieudumayet , 

> As default, it is set to 256. What does it actually mean? Is it the number of tokens question+passage combined?
If not, what is it?

It's the maximum sequence length for question and passage **individually**, i.e. long questions will be truncated to 256 tokens and similarly passages will be truncated to 256 tokens. We plan to switch this to individual params to give more fine-grained control (questions are usually way shorter than 256 tokens). 

> I divided my documents into passages which consist of less than 512 tokens each. So I wonder if I would set max_len_seq to be 256 and a passage is larger than 256 token, would DPR ignore half of each passage?

It would only ignore the part of the passage that is > 256 tokens."

Title: b'mathieudumayet'
Body:
b'Hey @tholor ,

Thank you for the explanation! BertTokenizer is the tokenizer that DPR uses, right? Because I will set **max_seq_len** parameter to 512 and divide documents into max. 512 tokens each. 

Best,
Mathieu'

Title: b'tholor'
Body:
b'> BertTokenizer is the tokenizer that DPR uses, right?

Yes

> Because I will set max_seq_len parameter to 512 and divide documents into max. 512 tokens each.

If you use a token-based split for your documents, I'd recommend splitting into something slightly smaller than 512.
You will need some extra space for the "special tokens" (e.g [CLS]). Also, in case you have meaningful "title" information attached to your documents, we will concatenate it to the "text" before truncating everything down to 512 (titles often boost the retrieval performance a bit). You can see the related code snippet here: 
https://github.com/deepset-ai/haystack/blob/4fa5d9c3eba860ef0a85c46465b9ff1902ebfa12/haystack/retriever/dense.py#L145-L152
  
'

Title: b'mathieudumayet'

Title: b'lalitpagaria'
Body:

There performance issue with transformers, but now it's has been fixed. https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/5811 . As mentioned in #337, you can use model with `TransformersReader`.

> Would model deliver a better answer if the number of tokens is high, because then it would understand the context better?

As per paper, pre-trained, Longformer consistently outperforms RoBERTa (but slightly ~1%-4%) on long document task and it is less complex than high performing GNN models. I feel (not 100% sure) it is good choice if you don't want to split docs much and store as it is into the document_store.
"

Title: b'tholor'
